speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a correction not so much of Hansard but of a misunderstanding between the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) and myself last night arising from our rather casual use of words. As reported at page 4467 of Hansard the hon. member for Cape Breton South said the national credit societies act was a government measure passed by this parliament. I asserted that was not so, that it was the bill of a private member to incorporate a credit union society under a federal charter. However, I was wrong. The bill I had in mind was not the national credit societies act but the Canadian Cooperative Credit Society Limited Act, a private bill passed in 1953 and sponsored by a private member, Mr. Bater. However, the hon. member for Cape Breton South was also wrong, for there is no such act as the national credit societies act. The act he probably had in mind is the Co-operative Credit Associations Act, a government-sponsored measure to control interprovincial activities of credit unions, passed earlier in 1953. Otherwise we were both right in that both these acts are important in the discussion which took place on the role that credit unions should take in the new fisheries improvement loans bill.
If I may add one final word, a couple of miners such as the hon. member for Cape Breton South and myself have at times been exasperated by the way lawyer members of
parliament quibble over words. This incident shows us the importance of exact legal terminology.

AMENDMENTS RESPECTING BOYS* INDUSTRIAL HOME, NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL REFORMATORY
The house resumed, from Monday, June 6, consideration in committee of Bill No. 381, to amend the Prisons and Reformatories Act-Mr. Garson-Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.
On clause 1-Boys under 16 years.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask your advice with respect to procedure on clause 1? In that clause it is set out that sections 110 to 120 of the Prisons and Reformatories Act, chapter 217 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, are repealed and other sections are substituted therefor. That is the only actual governing clause. Under that clause do we discuss all the amending clauses? Is that correct, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I have called clause 1, and it is of course in order to discuss any matter coming under clause 1 which apparently deals with a number of sections in the original enactment.

That being the case, I should like to speak on clause 1 with particular reference to what will now be known as sections 110 and 111.
On the second reading last night I asked a number of brief questions relative to a principle in the bill and asked the Minister of Justice if he would give a detailed explanation of that principle in the committee of the whole. After reading what I said in Hansard this morning, I realize I spoke far too briefly. Perhaps if I were to make my own position clear on this matter and state the reasons why I requested the minister to give us an exposition of that principle, my purpose would be served.
It has been my privilege, Mr. Chairman, in the past 22 years to have had some connection with boys' industrial schools, and in that

Prisons and Reformatories Act period of time not only to have interested myself in the cases of boys under the age of 16 who have been bad boys, but also upon occasion to have been called upon by judges in charge of juvenile courts and welfare courts in cases of boys who were incorrigible. As a result of that 22 years' experience and knowledge, as I said last night, I am a little bit disturbed by the principle which is outlined in clause 1 concerning what will be sections 110 and 111.
A youth under the age of 16 is without doubt at a very impressionable age. He makes a serious mistake and comes into conflict with the law. He appears in court. Now, once in a while you meet, and I have met, youths under the age of 16 with whom there is not a thing you can do. In the majority of cases, however, so far as my experience goes, when you have a boy of the age of 16 who has been arrested and brought into court, he is a very frightened boy. Under the terms of this bill and the two sections I have mentioned that youth, because he has broken the law and been arrested, can be charged with a crime as though he were an adult. I do not think there is any way we can get around that. But, Mr. Chairman, he can also be sentenced as though he were an adult. I do not think there is any way to get around that, at the moment at any rate.
But having been found guilty and sentenced, under the principle which I am now discussing, he can then be sent to a boys' industrial home. I feel, sir, that is as it should be because it would be a terrible thing if a boy under 16 were sent to a provincial jail or a penitentiary. I am in complete agreement with the attorney general of New Brunswick and the Minister of Justice on that. Once he has been found guilty and sentenced on a definite charge, we now find under the principle in this bill, it is possible that, having served his sentence and having paid his debt to society for the crime which he committed, he can then be sentenced by a judge to an indeterminate time in the boys' industrial school so long as the total sentence does not exceed five years.
Mr. Chairman, I want to make my position clear, and that is why I am on my feet again this afternoon in committee of the whole. I believe that, as applied to youthful offenders, the indeterminate sentence is best. That is my belief-although I realize there are arguments against it. The chief argument- there is really only one-against the indeterminate sentence, one which I have learned from conversations with boys in the industrial homes and with adult criminals in penitentiaries who are serving indeterminate sentences on charges of being habitual criminals,


is that they harbour a feeling of hatred against society and against the courts, a feeling of hatred against everybody, because they do not know when they can get out. I have yet to speak to one boy in a reformatory or one prisoner in a penitentiary, serving a sentence as a habitual criminal, who has not developed an aggressive hatred against society in general. They feel that they may be imprisoned for a month, or for life-they do not know which. Believing as we do in rehabilitation, in my opinion we make a mistake when we deny the many hope by withholding from them knowledge as to when they will again be free.
Referring more particularly to boys in reformatories, I said a few moments ago to the Minister of Justice, through you, Mr. Chairman, that it is my belief that, although these boys may not know whether they are going: to be in the reformatories for a month or for five years, the indeterminate sentence is best for those under 16 years. However, I do not approve of the way it is being carried out in one or two of the provinces, and as recommended in the act. Under clause 110 and clause 111 they are charged with a definite offence and given a definite sentence. Take a boy under 16 years of age. He is impressionable. At that time you can work with him, or you can with the great majority of boys. After they have been charged and sentenced, and have paid their debt to society, it is possible under this legislation to keep these boys in an institution for a period that shall not exceed five years. Ask any psychologist or any psychiatrist what he thinks will be the reaction of the majority of boys who have committed a crime and served their sentence and still cannot be released but may be held in the discretion of the judge or the parole board up to a period of five years.
I say, sir, most sincerely from my knowledge of working with boys in an industrial school for 22 years that that is not going to rehabilitate them; that is not going to make them socially conscious; that is not going to give them a feeling of friendship. I am sure it will build up aggressiveness and a hatred that can lead them down the road to further criminality. I completely realize what the minister and attorney general of New Brunswick have in mind. We must have a provision so that boys who are incorrigible or anti-social can be handled, disciplined and trained in an institution in the hope of making them good members of society. I agree with that; but, sir, I disagree with a provision under which a boy who is charged, found guilty and sentenced, and has served his term, can be kept in an institution. From the psychological point of view it will be far better

-and I commend this thought to the Minister of Justice-to have a different procedure with respect to boys under the age of 16. It should be one of two things. As I said last night on second reading of this bill, when a boy has served his sentence for the crime of which he has been found guilty he should then be released. If he is incorrigible, and if it is in the interests of the boy himself and society, he should remain in an institution. Then either his parents, the children's aid society, the welfare society or any government agency interested in the development of children could then bring him before the court as an incorrigible and give him an indeterminate sentence in the hope that a useful citizen can be made out of him. The boy would at least know that he had served his sentence and was being released.
There is one other approach which I favour even more than the one I have just mentioned. If a youth under 16 years of age breaks the law and is brought to court I suggest that a study be made of his background, his emotions and his outlook. If the boy is found guilty, instead of sentencing him to a period in an institution and then perhaps keeping him there after he has served his sentence, I suggest that he should be given an indeterminate sentence at the beginning. He would then know that his length of stay in the institution would depend upon his good behaviour and his adjustment.
Personally I believe that such a boy would feel better if he knew at the beginning that he was being given an indeterminate sentence and his length of stay would depend upon his attitude, his behaviour and his adjustment rather than to be given a definite sentence and then after having served it be told that he would be kept on for a further period after he had expiated his offence against society.
I must conclude, otherwise I shall be repeating myself. I feel deeply about this matter from the point of view of the psychological effect upon a youthful offender. I submit that the imposition of two sentences will not help to rehabilitate a boy under 16 years of age who has come into conflict with the law.
Secondly, I think it is a wrong concept of Canadian justice that when a boy is found guilty of a crime and sentenced he can still be retained in an institution up to a period of five years after he has expiated his crime. That is not my concept of Canadian justice.
I realize the motives of the Minister of Justice and the attorney general of New Brunswick, but I would ask the Minister of Justice if perhaps we are not making a mistake in an approach of this kind. I want
7.	1955	4485
Prisons and Reformatories Act the minister to understand that I believe sincerely in the indeterminate sentence; I think it is the best thing in the world. But let us have it as a first charge and not as a second one. Let us remember the psychological effect on a youth under 16 years of age when, having served his sentence, he cannot get out. I ask the minister if he will please give this approach some thought and if he will explain the reasons why, in his judgment and in the judgment of others, they bring in this kind of a recommendation.

Mr. Chairman, I too have some knowledge of boys. I have often been convinced that there is no bad boy. I have sat in juvenile court and in police stations and I have been convinced that the individual who should have been sent to court was not the boy but the father or the mother. Where a boy has a father and mother who spend a good deal of time in the beer parlour and let him go where he likes, who is guilty? I was well pleased when the Prime Minister, when he was minister of justice, said it is far better to give the prisoner-whether he is a boy or a grown-up-the benefit of the doubt and not ask him to serve his complete sentence.
I should not say it but I have had 183 boys and adults out on permit or parole and only 3 have partially failed. I have never had a boy placed under our supervision who failed. I agree with the hon. member who has said that it would be far better to let the boy know when he goes in that a good deal depends on his conduct. That is one side of it. But the other side of it is that the folks at home that know him, outside of the family, should keep an eye on him, write him his weekly letter and tell him that there is hope for him and that he should make good.
I am sure that the Minister of Justice will be just as lenient as was the former minister of justice in giving the boy the benefit of the doubt and in letting him come out under the supervision of somebody whose Christian character is known to be practical and who is not afraid to spend a little bit in his behalf.

Mr. Chairman, I listened with a great deal of interest to the hon. member for Vancouver East in the exposition he has just made on juvenile criminality. Certainly the arguments that he has advanced are cogent even though they are emotional as well. On the face of it, it seems that legislation such as this is more or less in keeping with the ideas of criminologists of 25, 30 or 40 years ago rather than of today.
As I listened to the arguments he advanced I tried to place myself for a moment, as one must, in the position of a juvenile offender who has been punished by the court for the
4486	HOUSE OF
Prisons and Reformatories Act wrong that he has committed. The initial punishment he receives is in keeping with the enormity of the crime he has committed. That punishment would be the punishment that would be administered to one of mature years. He starts off with that punishment.
Because of the fact that an indeterminate sentence commences after the termination of the fixed sentence, if I understand the authorities correctly, there can be no remission of part of the fixed sentence when it is to be followed by one that is indeterminate. The only reduction that can be made will be the reduction by the parole board of the sentence subsequently imposed and commencing at the termination of the original sentence. He is then in this position. He has paid his penalty to society in respect of the first sentence he has received. Then he starts all over again with a sentence that, as far as he is concerned, may be up to five years or may be shorter. That, of course, is something he does not know. In other words, there is no reward for virtue under this type of legislation.
If the juvenile has received a sentence of two years, under normal circumstances he should expect to be released at the end of a year and three or four months, with the balance of his sentence served outside the jail or penal institution and under parole. But the juvenile offender is not put in that position and is not today, in two jurisdictions, in that position. He must serve his two years. Then he starts all over again. To me that is a dangerous reincorporation in our law of a principle that is not in keeping with the advances that have been made in criminology in the last 25 years.
My friend the hon. member for Vancouver East has an experience that deserves the respect of parliament, in view of the degree to which he over the years has interested himself on behalf of those who are unfortunately in the penal institutions of this country. He points out that if the situation were reversed and if the first sentence were indeterminate, there would be a reward for reform. As the situation is now, the wrongdoer serves the sentence that any older person would serve; then having done that and having been denied the parole to which an older person would be entitled, he commences another sentence.
I feel that the minister should be able to place before the house and the committee suggestions arising out of the experience in the two jurisdictions that already have in effect similar legislation. I understand that Ontario is one of the provinces, and that there is another province with similar legislation


in effect, namely British Columbia. Will the minister place before the committee the following statistics? How many juveniles under this legislation have, in each of those provinces, received first a set sentence and thereafter an indeterminate sentence? Of those so sentenced, how many became recidivists or repeaters?
After all, the aim of the criminal law today is to punish but at the same time to reform; that is, the aim is to give to those who have made a wrong step an opportunity for rehabilitation, an opportunity to go forward in the world, raising their heads once more because, while they have made one wrong step, society is not going to condemn them indefinitely into the future. As a matter of fact, today one of the major reasons for recidivism, as I see it, is the fact that when a man serves a term in a penitentiary or a jail and then comes out, particularly in times when jobs are not available, the situation becomes impossible for him, there being not available to him any unemployment insurance for the time during which he was actually in employment before he committed his offence. He goes forth into the world unable to find a job and hanging over him there is the stigma of recent conviction. Instead of encouragement to resist temptation that becomes stronger because of his previous conviction, he finds once more that he is forced into the position of having again to commit crime. I have had some experience with those who have committed crime. I have appeared for the defence in several hundreds of cases. I have never had a client who repeated, but in every case where I have acted and the person has been convicted I have taken a personal interest in him when he has come out of jail. I did not mean to speak about that, Mr. Chairman. I do not want to deal with personal matters. But I do know I am proud of the fact that I have never had a repeater.
This comes about through the simple act of trying to give assistance, not monetary assistance but encouragement. It is no encouragement to an offender, whether young or old, to know that at the expiry of his sentence, when he has satisfied his debt to society, society may say: Well now, for an indefinite period of the next two or three years you are still going to be kept in custody until such time as you prove you have shown a tendency to reform. First you blot out any hope of reform from the fact that the person has served a two year sentence. Then, having blotted it out, you want to resurrect that hope and have him come forth a good citizen.
I ask the minister to give the statistics. They are available and will tell the story

whether or not this system has been successful in the jurisdictions where it has been tried. If it has, idealistic arguments have little place. If it has not, the hon. member for Vancouver East has graphically and powerfully placed before the house considerations that deserve the thoughtful respect of each and every one of us.

I should like to say a word or two on the bill, although not from the point of view that the hon. members for Prince Albert and Vancouver East have discussed it because I am not competent to do that. But I do want to say a word or two generally because I am interested in these industrial homes and in what they can and should be. I am principally interested in two phases more than any others. One concerns the educational facilities which are or are not and, if not, should be supplied. Another has to do with whether or not these places have the advantages of having trained psychologists attached to their staffs.
May I say here that when I questioned the previous minister of justice on the matter of trained psychologists in connection with our prisons and penitentiaries a number of years ago, I was surprised to learn that there was only one at that time and he was attached to Kingston penitentiary. Surely if it is necessary to have psychologists on the staffs of our high schools which are teaching boys and girls who are normal at least to the extent of not having committed any crime, there is an even greater need for the guidance of trained psychologists in industrial schools.
I am glad the bill has been introduced because its purpose ostensibly and actually is to advance the cause of penal reform in New Brunswick. A boy who might otherwise be given a sentence of three months or more in a penitentiary or common jail can now be sent to the boys' industrial home. If sent to the penitentiary he would have to mix with hardened criminals and sending him there would, in my opinion, simply defeat the purpose of the punishment. But an industrial home can be, and I emphasize "can", a source of individual rehabilitation and social redemption as far as the boy is concerned. Again, if a boy is sentenced for 14 days or more he can, by the decision of the judge, also be sentenced-
To five years.

-forthwith or at the expiration of the two weeks sentence, to a period in the industrial home. When I first read the bill I thought the boy had to serve the two weeks sentence first and would then be
Prisons and Reformatories Act further sentenced, but I see he may be sentenced forthwith or at the end of his imprisonment. Why that provision, "or at the expiration of his imprisonment", is in the bill I do not know. Perhaps the minister will be able to explain that to us. He may be sentenced forthwith or after the expiry of the short sentence to a period not exceeding five years in an industrial home. I do not want to trespass on the ground already covered by the hon. member for Vancouver East, but I suggest that pretty wide powers are given there involving great responsibility over the life of a boy up to a period of five years. I take it, of course, that the people under whose authority this is done are responsible people. I believe they are judges under the terms of the act.
Then there is to be a parole committee which will have the power to discharge a boy or to discharge him in the custody of someone who can give him employment. The latter can only be done with the consent of the parent or guardian of the boy. There is of course a danger there as to the type of employer. We have heard of a number of unfortunate cases. I do not need to go back into the classics to find an example. We find them every day in our newspapers. I warn the minister that there are still Simon Legrees about.
The hon. member for Vancouver East has emphasized the matter of environment and what it does to people. The hon. member for Fort William meant exactly the same thing when he said there are no bad boys, there are only bad parents. That is simply another way of saying that it is the environment surrounding the boy which is usually- I do not say always-to blame for the condition that has arisen. If environment has been the cause, then I suggest that environment must be the cure. That brings me back to my first words. For the benefit of my hon. friend, may I say I am not arguing for a moment that we should commit these boys for five years, but if we are going to do so we want to know the sort of place to which they are going to be committed. If environment is to be the cure then the home, wherever it is, must be a place of joy-yes, I say "joy"-and reformation and not a place where they will suffer further degradation, as has happened in the past.
There must also be educational facilities of such a type that when the boy leaves the industrial home he will not be at a disadvantage compared with those who have attended our ordinary schools. I say again that while the boy is there he should be in the care of those who can exercise guidance-I think that is the word they are using now-in the
4488	HOUSE OF
Prisons and Reformatories Act same way as in our ordinary high schools and universities. There should be guidance instructors or guidance teachers. While the boy is there he must have the benefit of guidance and training by men qualified in that particular profession.
I want to mention one more thing and that is the stigma of a jail sentence. I suppose it is rather difficult to get away from that. But I do suggest that if we are to do away with the stigma of a jail sentence or of any sentence, we must send these juvenile delinquents, as I say, to a place where there is actual happiness and to which there shall be no stigma attached in their own minds upon discharge.

I rise to speak briefly on this matter, Mr. Chairman, because as I listened to the discussion last evening it seemed to me that the interpretation then was somewhat different from the interpretation being placed on the bill this afternoon. Both the hon. member for Saint John and the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton representing the province of New Brunswick spoke on this bill at the second reading stage. It was my understanding from their remarks that this legislation was coming before the house on the basis of a recommendation from New Brunswick, and the suggestion was to bring the legislation in line with a program of modernizing the New Brunswick penal system. On the other hand, this afternoon there seems to be a feeling that this legislation is a retrograde step in the handling of juvenile delinquents in New Brunswick.
Now, as I have attempted to read the bill and follow the discussion, I was rather inclined to the viewpoint that this legislation was more in sympathy with the modern emphasis in criminology, that we should think in terms of reformative measures rather than punitive measures. The essential purpose of the bill seems to be to provide for the establishment of a central reformatory, a modern type of institution. I think that is a good step because one of the weak links in the chain of our penal institutions is the inadequately staffed and inadequately programmed local jails and, in many cases, provincial institutions.
I know that in my own province of Manitoba there has been considerable discussion on the problem created in our provincial institutions as a result of the lack of adequate facilities to carry out a modern program of penology. As I understand, the purpose of this bill is to provide for a modern type of institution that will make possible the more comprehensive approach to the problem of treating juvenile delinquents. I raise that


point because I should like to have a clarification from the Minister of Justice when he replies to the various points that have been raised in the discussion this afternoon. Either the bill is going to carry out the wishes of the government of New Brunswick or it is a retrograde step, as has been indicated in some of the remarks here this afternoon.
The second main purpose is to provide for a parole board. That is contained in what will be section 112 of the act. This section reads as follows:
The lieutenant-governor in council may appoint a parole committee whose duty it shall be to inquire from time to time into the cases of prisoners sentenced to the boys' industrial home, and where as a result of such inquiry the parole committee thinks proper, it may permit prisoners serving sentences in the boys' industrial home to be discharged on parole under conditions approved of by the Minister of Justice.
I am in favour of extending the system of granting paroles because I believe it is a much healthier approach to the problem. Particularly in the case of juvenile delinquents, we should be trying to reform them within society rather than trying to provide an artificial environment in a penal institution. Again it is my impression from the remarks of the two members from New Brunswick that the purpose of this legislation is to broaden the parole facilities and to emphasize the remedial rather than the punitive aspect of dealing with juvenile delinquents. The Minister of Justice will notice that I am putting this in the form of a query because I am in a bit of a quandary as to which is the right interpretation of the legislation, whether it is a retrograde step or whether it is actually going to deal with the reforms suggested by the province of New Brunswick.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, in the granting of parole facilities to the provincial government, I am wondering whether the supervision of the parolee under those circumstances comes directly under the provincial authorities or still falls back upon the federal authorities? I say that because if any program of parole is going to deal adequately with the situation there must be proper supervision and properly trained personnel. There must have been some form of rehabilitation program that will help in the transition from the life of the institution to life in free society. Provided the personnel are available and provided an adequate parole program is available, I would tend to feel that this legislation is a step in the right direction.
So far as the indeterminate sentence measure is concerned, I am wondering whether the emphasis in allowing for an indeterminate sentence is to make it possible to further punish the delinquent, or is it to

provide a longer period of time in order to apply a remedial and educational program? I would suggest it is much better, especially in the case of juvenile delinquents, to release them at the time when they are psychologically ready rather than subscribing to the philosophy that when their time has expired out they go, regardless of whether or not they are psychologically prepared. I would presume also that the indeterminate measure is there to allow a suitable time for completing any trade training that the juvenile delinquent may be undergoing within the institution. Again, if that is so, it is absolutely essential that the provincial authorities have adequate programs set up within the so-called modern institution.
I have presented all this somewhat in the form of a query because we seem to be at cross purposes as to the emphasis placed on the measure last night.

Before the minister replies, I have a question or two to which he might reply at the same time. Although I did not speak on second reading, I am inclined to favour the bill because I believe it is a step in the right direction in giving boys a chance when they recognize they have done wrong. I believe you cannot stereotype human nature. You cannot impose penalties and say we imposed that penalty on one boy a few months ago, and therefore we are going to impose the same penalty for the same crime on another boy. Perhaps from the legal point of view that is a reasonable approach; but from the point of view of human nature it may not necessarily be. I have had considerable experience in work among boys and have been in charge of a number of boys' camps. I have studied boys under those conditions and believe I have learned something about them. In my earlier experience the philosophy was held out to me that, in reality, there never was a bad boy. However, after having operated some of those camps I am inclined to the belief that that philosophy is wrong, and that there are bad boys. Of course the philosophy has its background in the thought that we should never look upon boys as being basically bad, and that we should keep in mind that under proper environment and as a result of proper training their lives can be shaped so that even those who may appear to be the worst may turn out very well indeed.
I remember one boy who had the habit of inflicting punishment upon animals. He would grab a cat, take out his knife, and cut its head off, just to see the reaction. At one time or another however in that boy's life he received a different kind of instruction, and because of that instruction 50433-283
Prisons and Reformatories Act and an improved environment he turned out to be one of the best young men in the community. As a matter of fact he became a medical doctor. Perhaps his experience in cutting the heads off cats gave him a good deal of practice.
I do not believe human nature can be stereotyped. This bill gives the boy a chance. It may be found that, after all, his punishment may have been a little too harsh, and it may be felt that with the proper adjustments in his life he may make a great improvement.
However, what I had intended to say at this time was along slightly different lines. All the reformatories in the world do not get at the basic or root causes of juvenile delinquency. I doubt very much whether we could introduce legislation that would deal adequately with this problem. I made reference to the subject last year when we were considering the minister's estimates. Perhaps in doing so I was slightly out of order, because I noticed that at the time the chairman was tremendously agitated. I did so however because there does not appear to be any place in the estimates or, in fact, anywhere else, where one could discuss in detail the subject of juvenile delinquency, and suggest a remedy for it.
I suggest that it could be done under the administration vote in the minister's estimates.

Perhaps so; I am not going to argue the point. I have always made the claim that nothing could happen in Canada that would not find its place under some department of government, upon which responsibility could be focused. But when it comes down to certain principles of life it seems that we cannot legislate, and it becomes very difficult to know what action to take.
I claim that the solution to the problem of juvenile delinquency is not that of dealing with it when it is upon us. Rather, the basic solution is to deal with it before it becomes juvenile delinquency. Therefore I claim the home is greatly responsible for the situation, and it is something concerning which we cannot legislate. Not long ago I read an article stating that the wave of juvenile delinquency in these days could be traced to the condition during the war years, when mothers and fathers were working, or fathers were away and mothers had to assume all the responsibilities of the homes. It was suggested that under those conditions children did not have the chance they should have in their own homes, and it was pointed out that

Prisons and Reformatories Act the war was responsible for the juvenile delinquency which followed.
This contention can be overemphasized, in my opinion. I believe we have to focus responsibility upon home and school life. Some service clubs have taken an active interest in this respect and have done marvellous work. It is unfortunate that we cannot appropriate more money to organizations of that kind, with a view to preventing juvenile delinquency.
However, when this condition develops it must be dealt with. The minister is taking the proper procedure in this bill when he gives the boy or the girl a chance. When it is found that proper environment and proper direction can help these young people, and that lives can be saved, it is only proper that they be given that environment and direction.
Let me say at once that I have no use for any process of mollycoddling. In my view when people commit wrongs they should be punished.
Is the hon. member in favour of two punishments for one crime?

No, I am not in favour of two punishments for one crime. I believe that when the penalty is meted out, and when that penalty has been paid, then the debt to society is cancelled. However, I do not look upon this bill as making provision for two punishments.
That is my only point.

I agree with my hon. friend on that. Referring again to my reference to mollycoddling, there are some who believe that only kindness should be shown in the treatment of crime. I do not think that is so. There are times when firmness must be shown, while at the same time showing a measure of kindness.
At this point I would ask the minister a question. Perhaps he would be prepared to discuss the matter at some greater length, because most of us are not too well informed about reformatories. I believe that the personnel of these reformatories must be very carefully chosen. If you get men in boys' reformatories or women in girls' reformatories who are going to be great big bosses and nothing more than bosses, who are going to throw their weight around and take it out on the boys just to be spiteful or to get their own way, that is not the way to handle them. I have found from experience that sometimes you can take a very bad boy who is upsetting the whole works by his attitude and give him some responsibility. He exercises that responsibility. He feels that he counts


for something, and through that responsibility you can sometimes overcome the problem that he himself is making.
All I am saying here is that trained and efficient personnel should be chosen for the particular positions in those reformatories, but at the same time having due regard for everything. Their chief function should be to see whether they cannot make something out of the life of the boy or girl. If they are there simply to hold down a job and to see that the inmates are regimented, that they are in at night at a certain time and to act as big bosses, then they will not reform the children. That is my own view.
I note that the parole board is chosen by the provincial government. Can the minister throw light on the method that the parole board uses in determining what parole should be given? Do they interview the boy or the authorities? Is it paper work? Just what method is used?
I do not think I need to take up any more time of the committee. I have expressed my ideas. I do emphasize once again that you will not get rid of juvenile delinquency by all your prisons or all your penalties in the world. There has to be something basic in it. It has to be tackled at its source.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wanted to hear and reply to all criticisms; but perhaps I might have shortened the debate somewhat if I had risen to my feet earlier in the discussion, and I am at fault to some extent for not having done so. Several of those who have taken part in the debate have proceeded quite sincerely upon what I must regard as a misconception of the arrangement that is envisaged in this proposed legislation.
But before I deal with this point perhaps I had better answer the question which has just been asked of me by the hon. member for Macleod. He asked what are the conditions under which parole would be granted by a provincial parole board appointed under this proposed legislation. I do not think I can do much better by way of a reply to that question than to read the conditions of the licence-that is the term used, the parole licence-which is issued by the British Columbia parole board under a provision in the Prisons and Reformatories Act, dealing with that province. They are as follows:
1.	The licensee,-
That is the parolee.
-during the term of his licence, shall be under the supervision and authority of the provincial probation officer.
2.	He shall proceed to such place and remain in the care of such person as is directed by the provincial probation officer and shall not move

from that place or change his residence without the consent of the provincial probation officer or the person under whose care he has been placed.
3.	He snail obey such instructions as may be given him and shall report periodically as and when directed.
4.	He shall abstain from any violation of the law.
5.	He shall not habitually associate with notoriously bad characters, such as reputed thieves and prostitutes.
6.	He shall not lead an idle and dissolute life without visible means of obtaining an honest livelihood.
7.	He shall preserve his licence and produce it when called upon to do so by a magistrate or peace officer.
Then there is a provision for further conditions to be inserted at the bottom, applicable to the specific person named in the licence.
I said during the debate on the second reading of the bill, by way of a suggestion to the hon. member for Vancouver East, that I thought the reason for this provision would emerge if he would read slowly and aloud the clause which is under discussion. Perhaps I had better indicate the sincerity of my suggestion by following that course myself. Clause 111 reads:
Where any boy, apparently under the age of 16 years, is convicted of an offence punishable by law on summary conviction, and thereupon is sentenced and committed to prison in any common jail for a period of not less than 14 days, any judge of the supreme court or a county court, in any case occurring within the county or counties for which he is such judge, may examine and inquire into the circumstances of such case and conviction, and when he considers that the material and moral welfare of the boy requires such sentence, he may, as an additional sentence for such offence, sentence such boy, either forthwith or at the expiration of his imprisonment in such Jail, to the boys' industrial home, to be there detained for the purpose of his industrial and moral education for an indefinite period, not exceeding in the whole five years from the commencement of his imprisonment in the common jail.
The clauses of this section that require emphasis are these. When the judge "considers that the material and moral welfare of the boy requires such sentence", he may sentence the boy to be detained in the industrial home "for the purpose of his industrial and moral education for an indefinite period not exceeding in the whole five years". I must confess thatvMr. Winch:	As additional to the offence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, as an additional sentence.
To the offence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am afraid that I do not
get my hon. friend's point.

The minister emphasized certain clauses. I am asking him to emphasize the part which appears halfway down the clause as follows: "As an additional sentence for such offence."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The language to which my
hon. friend refers is necessitated by the fact that the only way under our law in which one free man can lawfully interfere with another free man's freedom is by virtue of such a provision in the law as that under which an accused who has been found guilty can be sentenced and thereby deprived of his liberty for a period of time, determinate or indeterminate, not to exceed a prescribed limit, by reason of the offence that he has committed. It is perfectly clear in this legislation that the real reason for the indeterminate sentences for these boys of an age of less than 16-
Mr. Chairman,-*

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will let me' finish the sentence, or the idea, then he can ask all the questions he likes. The real reason for this indeterminate sentence is to provide for the boy's welfare. The section says that the judge may do this in view of the circumstances of the case, and for the purpose of his moral and industrial education.
Let us take a concrete case of a young lad, we shall say, of 14 years of age who is brought before a magistrate for what may be a pretty minor and frivolous offence such as stealing a banana from a fruit stand, or something of that kind. They might let him off with a suspended sentence and without sending him to an industrial home, or jail, without taking his liberty away at all. But supposing the police who arrested the boy find on inquiry that the home he comes from and the environment in which he lives make it seem to be quite likely that this first offence is but the beginning, that if he continues to live in that environment he is headed for a really serious criminal career.
Under those circumstances it seems to me that while the offence itself might not be serious-if you will read the section you will see that where a boy is committed to a prison for not less than 14 days, that is anything above 14 days in the way of a determinate sentence, that is sufficient justification for an indeterminate sentence-the intelligent thing to do is to have that boy taken away from this unfavourable environment in which he is living and put in an industrial home where he can be properly trained. I am surprised to hear the hon. member for Vancouver East,

Prisons and Reformatories Act object to this procedure. I had always understood that in his humane attitude towards prisoners he had thought-and I must say that if I correctly appraise his thoughts I agree with him-that the real function of all prisons should be, not so much to punish as to rehabilitate. It is true that prisons are provided for the security of society; but if we do not rehabilitate in the prisons and merely treat the prisoner's incarceration as punishment, then the security to society that we provide is very temporary and in many cases will cease the minute the man is released from prison.
I appreciate what the minister is saying and his interpretation of my views on rehabilitation is absolutely correct. As I understand it, the minister is discussing the new section 111. -

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am attempting to reply to a number of hon. members. I have no objection to my hon. friend from Vancouver East putting a question, but I should like to preserve some sort of continuity in my remarks and would appreciate that my hon. friend should not make a number of speeches in interruption of my own remarks.
Is the minister not referring to section 111?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If my hon. friend wishes to ask a question I shall be glad to answer, but I would prefer that he should not interrupt me in order to make another speech.

Section 111 deals with summary convictions under which a boy may be sentenced to a short term, but then, and I quote, there can be an additional sentence for such offence. I ask the Minister of Justice how that additional sentence of up to five years can be imposed on summary conviction which is for not over two years. Where in the law do you find that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend will find it in the language of the section he has just quoted. That is what this section says; and that supports the argument I have been making. It makes it abundantly clear that where a boy has been convicted of a summary offence for which he may be imprisoned for only 14 days the judge, where he sees that the facts warrant it, may order that the boy be detained in an industrial home for an indeterminate period not exceeding in the whole five years.
Does any person suppose that this indeterminate sentence is really a punishment so much as it is an attempt at the rehabilitation of that boy in perhaps the only way in which it can be brought about? If the boy comes from a broken home, say with a drunken
IMr. Garson.]
father and a prostitute mother, it does not strike me as being a very intelligent disposition of his case to put him in prison for 14 days and then let him return to that evil kind of environment.
Would not the boy have a better place to sleep and have better food to eat when he goes to that place?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Of course he would have. In addition to that he would receive proper training. My observation has been that most criminals come from unhappy homes. During their childhood they have lacked that kind and intelligent care which would be given in an industrial home even though on an institutional basis. If you examined these cases, as I had to do in connection with the duties I discharged when we did not have a solicitor general handling the federal Department of Justice remissions, you would find that in a great majority of cases the men and women who are criminals have had an unhappy home in their childhood.
Even though the parents are poor, if there are a loving and respectable mother and father the child usually gets a good start in life. But even with wealthy parents, if there is no love and respect in the home the child gets a bad start. When therefore we come here with a provision of this sort I would have thought the hon. member for Vancouver East would have been the first member to support it.
If it is the first sentence, yes. I have said that twice now, that the first sentence should be the indeterminate sentence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have listened to this discussion as to the difference between a primary indeterminate sentence and the indeterminate sentence being imposed afterward. I must say that I find it to be a rather quibbling sort of argument. If the determinate sentence is 16 days and the indeterminate sentence lasts three years, what difference does it make with regard to the three-year period that it was preceded by 16 days?
None.
It certainly does.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In all these amendments to the Prisons and Reformatories Act, as I went to some trouble to explain on the second reading of this bill in order that there would not be any misunderstanding as to just what function we are performing in this connection, we are dealing with legislation which has to do with the administration of provincial institutions. We are overcoming a certain difficulty under our constitution by providing in this case federal

legislation for the government of New Brunswick which after careful consideration that government has asked us to provide.
That being so, I think that unless there is some clear evidence to the contrary we are bound to take the position that in asking for this legislation the provincial government of New Brunswick, which is a responsible body, was acting properly and within its rights. Unless therefore we have some cogent reasons which are quite apparent on the surface for thinking they are quite wrong in regard to this particular section we should grant it in the form in which they have asked for it.
In this connection, what are the facts? This section under discussion is not, as would seem to be indicated by some of the arguments we have heard, the product of some new brainstorm that has overtaken the government of New Brunswick in the last few weeks. As I indicated on the second reading of the bill, this industrial home for boys was set up in 1893. If the hon. member for Vancouver East and the other hon. members who have taken part in the debate will look at the legislation of that time they will see that this provision which we are discussing has been in our act since 1893. If it were subject to the abuses which are now attributed to it one would have thought that they would have become apparent long since.
There have been changes in thinking by 1955.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Certainly there have been changes in thinking by 1955. But I suggest quite sincerely to my hon. friend-who I think himself is of the same view-that, so far as this particular section is concerned, the concept that a juvenile delinquent who is the product of a bad home environment should be taken from that environment and put into a proper institution is one with which I am sure he would agree. It is certainly one with which I agree.
I have made that point clear all down the line.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am saying that. I am giving my hon. friend full marks. That is why I say I cannot understand why he is opposed to this section.
On the procedure.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As to the procedure, what difference does it make whether there is this determinate sentence and then the indeterminate sentence?

It makes a great deal of difference.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Moreover, I would point out that this provincial parole board, which will be set up under the legislation we have before us here, will be made up of responsible citizens. It will operate under conditions which will be fixed by myself as Minister of Justice similar to those which I read to the committee a few minutes ago. If this provincial parole board had any reason to suppose that the juvenile who was serving this indeterminate sentence in the industrial home was not making the progress he should make, or if for any other reason that might occur to the parole board it thought he should be released, I am sure it would be glad to release him. But I am also sure that if the boy had an evil home environment there is small likelihood that the board would release him from the industrial home to go back to that evil environment.
The question may be asked-I think it was the hon. member for Saskatoon who raised it-whether this industrial home was to be properly staffed. In that connection I think probably I could not do better than read this letter. I may say that this is a different letter from the one I read on Friday. It is a letter which we received from the government of New Brunswick back in 1953 at the time they were considering the setting up of this industrial home. This letter reads as follows:
In 1949, the child welfare officials of this province expressed such concern with respect to the spreading of juvenile delinquency that the provincial government appointed a committee to investigate the conditions leading to delinquency and to recommend methods of dealing with delinquents.
The report of the committee, under the chairmanship of Miss Bessie F. Touzel, assistant director of the Canadian Welfare Council, Ottawa, recommended a number of important changes in the legislation respecting this subject.
The Boys Industrial Home Act, chapter 22 of the revised statutes of New Brunswick, 1952, was accordingly amended at the 1953 session of the legislature to conform to recommendations contained in the committee's report.
In other words, legislation was put through the New Brunswick legislature to make in this home the administrative changes that are the counterparts of the federal legislation which is required to cover the question of the detention of convicted persons under the Canadian Criminal Code so they may be legally received and detained in that home. I quote again:
The boys industrial home, which is specifically designated in part V of the Prisons and Reformatories Act as the place of imprisonment for the purposes of the act, was established by provincial iegislation in 1893 as a reformatory prison, and a "governing board" was constituted a body corporate for the ourpose of its administration.

Prisons and Reformatories Act
The amendments made to the Boys Industrial Home Act during the last session of the legislature are, in short, as follows:
(a)	The governing board of the boys industrial home, referred to in part V of the Prisons and Reformatories Act, has been dissolved and the administration of the home confined to the minister of health and social services.
In other words, it is directly responsible to a minister of the crown in the New Brunswick government. The letter continues:
(b)	The home is now described as a reformatory or industrial home, rather than as a reformatory prison as heretofore.
Then listen to this:
(c)	The aims of the home are now confined to-
Not detention or imprisonment.
-the education, industrial training and moral reclamation of juvenile delinquents.
(d)	The act, as amended, provides for the establishment of an advisory board and a parole committee.
The board and the committee have since been established.
In keeping with the recommendations of the Touzel report, every effort is being made to provide the boys industrial home with trained personnel. The appointment of a new superintendent is pending;-
I think this answers the question raised by the hon. member for Macleod.
-the appointee, a trained clinical psychologist, will be assisted by a psychiatric social worker. These two officials are already on the staff of the department of health and social services.
However, the boys confined to the home will not fully benefit from the improvements adopted by the province of New Brunswick since most of them are committed for violation of the Criminal Code of Canada and as such are subject, almost exclusively, to part V of the Prisons and Reformatories Act.
Then, in order to carry out these reforms which have been authorized by the provincial legislation, since they also come under the federal Prisons and Reformatories Act, he says this and I again quote:
T therefore request that consideration be given to amending part V of the Prisons and Reformatories Act so as to make all the provisions of the Boys Industrial Home Act applicable in all respects to juveniles committed for violation of the laws of Canada.		
I am enclosing copies of the Boys Industrial Home Act, with amendments, together with a copy of the recommendations made by the "parole committee". These recommendations have been approved in principle by the minister of health and social services and myself.
Under these circumstances, Mr. Chairman, it seemed to us that the requests of the government of New Brunswick were fair, wise and proper. Indeed, I cannot find much higher praise for them than to say that they meet the views of the hon. member for Vancouver East in respect of the proper treatment of juvenile offenders, namely a treatment that is rehabilitative in character and not merely punitive. That being so I plead-[DOT] and I think with good cause-for the support
[Mr. Garson.l
of the hon. member for Vancouver East and the other members who have spoken to the reforms which are covered by these suggested amendments.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with a great deal of attention to the remarks made by the Minister of Justice. On rehabilitation I of course agree with him 100 per cent. With the remarks of the attorney general which he has just quoted from the letter, I of course agree 100 per cent. There is no question about that whatsoever.
I have always had the highest regard for the Minister of Justice and I am rather disappointed at the line he has taken just now. He knows that not only I but all of us agree on all this approach, with regard to advancement, plans for rehabilitation and for taking care of the young. When I spoke on second reading last night and again this afternoon in this committee, at no time whatsoever did I criticize the advances provided for in this bill nor did I oppose the bill as a bill or criticize the question of rehabilitation. I have consistently raised only one point and the Minister of Justice unconsciously, shall I say-because I do not think he would do it deliberately-has kept completely clear of and away from the only point that I have raised.
I notice he has spent all his time on what will be section 111, having to do with summary conviction, but has made no mention at all of the new section 110 under which much heavier sentences can be imposed. I do not want to repeat. I have only one query, and it is the only one I have ever raised. It has to do with the psychological effect on a boy under the age of 16 who is charged with an offence under the law, found guilty, sentenced to a definite term and then having paid his debt to society, finds himself in the position of having a further sentence imposed in the discretion of a judge, which sentence can keep him in an institution up to five years.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Would he, as in many cases is the only other alternative, send the boy back to the bad environment from which he came?

I am afraid that the Minister of Justice either did not listen to what I said last night or has not listened to what I have been saying this afternoon. As a matter of fact, I was called out of order by the Speaker last night when I tried to speak about environment as it affects criminals in this country, and especially as it affects our youth.

The minister will realize 1 was called out of order last night when I tried to speak on that very matter. I want to know, and the minister has not answered me yet, under what law, what phase of Canadian justice, is a person found guilty of the same offence twice? The minister partially explained that by the fact that it is being done by this legislation. I maintain that is not right. If a boy is guilty of an offence, find him guilty, sentence him, let him serve his sentence and then release him.
I come to what the Minister of Justice asked me. He wanted to know if I would send the boy back to the same environment. The answer is no. If it is wrong for the boy to go back to that environment then remove him from it not on the basis that he has served his sentence on the charge on which he was found guilty but on the basis that he should be removed from the environment as a delinquent, as a bad boy, as a boy needing the opportunity of education and training.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Read the section.
I have read it and I know it. In sections 110 and 111 you find him guilty first-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Will my hon. friend permit a question?
Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What does he think that language means?
Where?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In section 111, the section we are discussing. It reads:
. . . such judge, may examine and inquire into the circumstances of such case and conviction, and when he considers that the material and moral welfare of the boy requires such sentence, he may-
And so on.
Read the "and so on".

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Certainly. I will read the whole thing.
-as an additional sentence for such offence, sentence such boy, either forthwith or at the expiration of his imprisonment in such jail, to the boys' industrial home, to be there detained for the purpose of his industrial and moral education for an indefinite period, not exceeding in the whole five years from the commencement of his imprisonment in the common jail.
The point I would emphasize again, and which I think the hon. member for Vancouver East is overlooking, is that this is not done except where the judge considers on examination of the circumstances of the case that the material and moral welfare of the boy requires such further detention in
Prisons and Reformatories Act the industrial home for the purpose of his industrial and moral education. So far as these purposes are concerned, I cannot imagine any that would be more worth while.

Mr. Chairman, this is one of the weirdest situations in which I have ever found myself in my 22 years' experience. I am convinced the minister and I are not far apart and yet at the same time we are worlds apart because the minister will not recognize what I am trying to tell him, that as an additional sentence for such offence the judge can do so and so and so and so. I am trying to point out that from the psychological point of view that is dynamite in the case of a boy at that impressionable age under 16. How many times do I have to tell the minister that it should be put as an indeterminate sentence to meet exactly what the minister wants, but do not leave it so that the boy will feel that he has been sentenced, has served his term and is still there.
I can assure the minister and all other members of the house that it is not going to rehabilitate psychologically a boy under 16 when he can be sentenced to a definite term and then receive an additional sentence up to five years. It will not help in the case of those who come under section 110 which is taken from the Criminal Code. It will not help a boy who has received a sentence of two years or more to find that, having served his definite sentence, he still has more years to serve on an indeterminate basis. I am going to quit. The minister and I are very close together on what we desire, but I am convinced that the minister is missing out on the procedural effect. That is all I am asking him to consider.
As I said last night and this afternoon, I welcome the bill as an advance in Canadian penology. I most sincerely welcome the letters expressing the approach and views of the attorney general of New Brunswick. He should be most highly commended. But I feel a mistake is being made in sections 110 and 111, and surely it is our responsibility in the House of Commons to point out a possible improvement.

I have a question or two I should like to put to the minister. When is the boy sentenced to the additional term? Is it at the time of the trial? Or after he has served his first sentence is the case again brought before a judge for review and the possible imposition of an additional sentence?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think the terms of the section make that quite clear. It reads:
Where any boy, apparently under the age of 16 years, is convicted of an offence punishable by law on summary conviction, and thereupon-
