Sentence will be imposed right after conviction.
-is sentenced and committed to prison in any common jail for a period of not less than 14 days, any judge of the supreme court or a county court, in any case occurring within the county or counties for which he is such judge, may examine and inquire into the circumstances of such case and conviction, and when he considers that the material and moral welfare of the boy requires such sentence, he may, as an additional sentence for such offence, sentence such boy . . .
The boy could come up for sentence before a magistrate, and if my hon. friend will examine section 111 he will see that it is only a judge of the supreme court or a county court who has the authority to impose this indeterminate sentence. It would have to be done, therefore, after the boy had been before the magistrate because first of all there must be a primary, determinate sentence imposed by the court before which the boy is found guilty, and then a subsequent inquiry by a supreme court or county court judge into the circumstances of his case.
May I ask the minister whether or not the accused has the benefit of counsel at this subsequent hearing resulting in the indeterminate sentence?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I certainly think there is no doubt at all that he has the privilege of having counsel. I do not think I could honestly say that in every case in which a juvenile came up he would be assured of counsel unless perhaps the bar association in New Brunswick, as they do in my own province, have a board set up for the purpose of seeing that prisoners are represented by counsel in all cases, whether or not they can afford it. I must say I do not know whether or not that exists in New Brunswick. He has the right to have counsel, that is certain.

It seems to me that the point the hon. member for Vancouver East is raising is an objection to committal other than by due process of law. In other cases in which there is a committal it is always after a trial in which the individual has all the privileges of counsel. I should think that this would be a very important consideration, that no individual be committed to any institution on any type of sentence unless somewhat the same formalities are carried out as in a regular trial.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
So far as the procedure in the administration of justice to which my hon. friend has referred in New Brunswick is concerned, it will be appreciated that those are provisions that would have to be made there as a matter of practice. In any event, I would think it would be a most extraordinary thing
[Mr. Garson.l

for a supreme court judge of that province or a county court judge to ever make an order of this kind without the most careful investigation. You see, the investigation he makes is into the circumstances of the case. How did the boy come to do this? What was his background and his environment? I cannot imagine a judge making an order of that kind without the most careful and exhaustive investigation, even if there were no counsel there at all.

I think the difficulty has arisen here in the matter of interpretation. I support fully the preference which seems to have been expressed for the indeterminate sentence. The difficulty seems to be the objection to what has been termed two sentences for one criminal act. I have read these two sections carefully, and I would ask the minister if this interpretation is not really the true meaning of section 110, and the reason why the expression occurs, "may further sentence"?
Using the example of the hon. member for Prince Albert, where a person is convicted of a crime carrying a sentence of two years, who would then be released on parole after serving a term of probably a year and three or four months, does this not mean that the person is, in effect, given an indeterminate sentence? He could not be released at a time earlier than one year and three or four months. In other words, after he serves a sentence appropriate to the offence for which he has been primarily committed, he can be paroled?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In other words, what my hon. friend is saying is, does he not have to serve his primary determinate sentence in full before any probation can be exercised in relation to the indeterminate sentence? No, I think not. I listened carefully to what the hon. member for Prince Albert said and I will grant that in cases which have to do with adults where there is a primary sentence, determinate sentence and a further indeterminate sentence, the cases are exceedingly exceptional, if indeed there are any, in which the remission board grants a remission in respect of the determinate sentence until it has been served in full, knowing there is in addition to that an indeterminate sentence.
One of the reasons for that is, as my hon. friend may know, that most of these indeterminate sentences are imposed in respect of people who have been convicted as habitual criminals. There are not very many of them and there are not many indeterminate sentences. But when an indeterminate sentence of that kind is imposed upon a man convicted of being an habitual criminal he has always

a record as long as your arm, he is usually a very desperate criminal, and there is no basis in fact for the granting of any remission, either of the determinate or indeterminate sentence. In other words, it does not arise from the rule that was referred to by the hon. member for Prince Albert which was, as I understood it, that having imposed a determinate and indeterminate sentence you could not remit in connection with the determinate sentence until it was fully served. It arises rather from the fact you very seldom have grounds for the exercise of any remission, in the case of an adult habitual criminal, in relation to either the determinate or indeterminate sentence.
In the case of a juvenile it would seem to me quite clear that if a boy were sentenced to a year determinate and another two years indeterminate, or three or four years indeterminate so the total would not be more than the five years indicated, then if at the end of six months perhaps the parole board had evidence brought before it whereby they were assured that this lad could get out of the industrial home and get a job with a farmer who was willing to take him and where he would have loving care, then I do not think they would have the slightest hesitation about granting parole. But as I apprehend it the main purpose of this whole legislation is that if there are no families that will take these boys, if there is no other environment in which they can be placed, at least they will be assured of the kind of environment which the industrial home will supply them. This will provide them with a decent chance in life. The thing we have to keep in our minds above all else in considering this legislation is that we are not dealing with adults, we are dealing with children. We are trying to provide that they shall not, if they have been convicted of an offence, ever have a worse environment than that which the industrial home provides.

May I ask a question? I hope I am not out of order, Mr. Chairman. Would the Minister of Justice consider moving that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again, in view of the fact that a committee meeting of the greatest importance in which he and I are both concerned has been called for 4.30?

Before that is decided, Mr. Chairman, may I say that for the past two days I have listened carefully to all the arguments and for the life of me I cannot see that the hon. member for Vancouver East, whom I esteem very deeply especially in this particular matter, has really explained what his grievance is. I agree entirely with 50433-284
Prisons and Reformatories Act what he says about the psychological effect of indeterminate sentences, and what seems to be the imposition of a double sentence. Surely, the whole purpose of what we are trying to do here is to validate some legislation that has been requested by New Brunswick. What New Brunswick is asking for is exactly what has been in effect in Alberta and Ontario.
While my lawyer colleagues in the house may not like this term, I think that sometimes when you make laws you have to have a legal subterfuge to achieve certain good things. I think the end that is being achieved by the two sections in dispute, sections 110 and 111, is entirely the end that the hon. member for Vancouver East wants to achieve. It seems to me what he objects to is what seems to be the power of a judge to inflict a second sentence at the end of the determinate period. When you come down to reality, surely what it is in practice is that the judge, for the sake of the boy or the girl, can keep that boy or girl away from an environment that would do injury to that boy or girl. But when'we come down to reality, surely what it is in actual practice is that a judge, for the sake of the boy himself, or for the girl, as the case may be, is keeping that boy or girl away from an environment that would be injurious. So it seems to me that if we had the complete privilege of wording the act as we would like to word it, we might have done so in such a way that it would not have caused such unnecessary conflict. However, I for one cannot see any difference between what the hon. member for Vancouver East is trying to get and what the Minister of Justice is giving us in this legislation.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with interest, and for two reasons, to the discussion of this matter. I have listened, first, because apparently the measure is intended to combat juvenile delinquency, which is a very important problem in Canada today. In the second place, I have before me an article which appeared in the Vancouver Province of May 30, bearing the heading "To the Penitentiary at Fourteen". It states in part as follows:
A 14 year old British Columbia boy has been sentenced to two years in the penitentiary for car theft.
The brief Canadian Press story about the sentencing of this lad had little to say about his case, except that he was one of four pyjama-clad youths who escaped from Brannen Lake school for boys a few days ago.
We do know, however, that when he appeared before Magistrate L. Beevor-Potts in Nanaimo he pleaded to be sent to the penitentiary because "at least I'll learn something there."

Prisons and Reformatories Act
This, apparently, indicates the expressed desire of a youth who found himself in the toils of the law, when he said he wanted to learn something that might be of some particular value to him. No doubt this is not the only boy who has recognized his difficult position and asked that something should be done for him. The fact that this boy has indicated a desire to learn, while being sent to a penitentiary, is most important indeed.
For this reason I would be most sympathetic toward the bill. I raised a question earlier because I felt there must be some way of getting around the principle of the double sentence. If the clauses are read carefully, as the minister has suggested, then every individual will be made to understand that a possible five-year sentence is facing him. That is a most important factor. Under those circumstances I would suggest that possibly the offender should be sentenced to an indeterminate sentence of five years.
To a reformatory.

Such sentence would be subject to review at a particular time, as stated by the judge who passed the sentence. It might be, of course, a magistrate who would sentence the individual to two weeks to begin with. It could not be done by a magistrate, because an indeterminate sentence of five years would not be permitted from him. But whoever sentenced the individual could ask for a review by the parole board at the end of two weeks, or a month, or two years, as the case might be. At that time it might be decided to set a later date at which the sentence could be reviewed, if it was found that the boy was making headway, that he was learning, or that it was hoped he might do so.
I would support the hon. member for Vancouver East so far as his contention regarding the psychological effect is concerned. A person who has paid for his crime has the right to feel that he will be free and able to continue his life with his old friends. If that boy were then to find that he was to be brought before a judge and sentenced to another five years, as an indeterminate sentence, it would simply sour his attitude towards society. I do not think we would be treating such an individual properly. I would ask the minister to give some consideration to the suggestion I have made, in the hope that something might be done.
There is one other question the minister might consider. Is there similar legislation in effect in any other province of Canada; if so, in what province or provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I realize the hon. member does not have the federal statutes in front of him.
However, if he would look at section 52 of the Prisons and Reformatories Act as passed by this parliament he would see that similar legislation is in effect in Ontario, that it is found in section 137 of the Manitoba part of this act, in section 92(6) of the Nova Scotia part and section 142 of the British Columbia part of this act limited to girls only.

In view of the fact that it is in effect in British Columbia, if it is working properly I am wondering why a child of 14 would ask to be sent to a British Columbia penitentiary so that at least he could learn something, as is indicated in the editorial in the Vancouver Province of May 30.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am afraid I could not answer or give explanations about an individual case in any province. In such a case there may be a number of circumstances that would make a certain course seem the wise one. However, since I do not know anything about the case to which the hon. member referred, I could not comment upon it intelligently.

Mr. Chairman, this discussion has extended over a wide field. However, after listening to the minister's explanation I cannot see very much to worry about. I am not absolutely or 100 per cent familiar with the intention in this instance, or with the details of carrying out reformation procedure in New Brunswick.
I do think, however, that hon. members who have spoken about sections 110 and 111 have overlooked section 112. It is the new section that gives the protection, because it gives the provincial authority the right to set up a parole committee which will review cases from time to time, or as often as required. All these institutions will be under the supervision of a person to be known as the inspector of penal institutions. He is to be a trained man and will be in charge of county jails, the industrial home for boys and the central reformatory. It will be his duty to see that in connection with detention there will be associated the idea of reform, education and rehabilitation rather than that of punishment.
This principle was expressed clearly in the letters read by the Minister of Justice. My reading of sections 110 and 111 does not indicate that a judge or a magistrate would give a sentence for a definite period and then bring the boy back and give him a further indeterminate sentence. It is all done at the same time, and I doubt if one boy or girl in a hundred would know there was a fixed period of detention with an indefinite period added. It would mean to them that they would be detained for a certain length of
fMr. Hahn.]

time; then, under section 112, whether they are detained for a fixed period, or a fixed period plus an indefinite period, their case may be reviewed.
That is my interpretation. If I am wrong in that I am sure the minister will correct me. As I say, that is the intention of the clause. If that is so, then we are causing ourselves a lot of worry and taking up a lot of time on this bill which is not necessary. This legislation was given a great deal of thought before the Department of Justice was asked to present it. I have faith in those in charge of the administration of justice in New Brunswick; I am sure the legislation will be carried out with the idea of reform, education and rehabilitation in mind, and that is what we are all after.

the second reading of Bill No. 256, to amend the Defence Production Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is a simple bill containing only two sections. The first section provides that the salary of the minister shall be $15,000 per annum. At the present time the salary of the minister is $10,000 per annum, but unfortunately the present minister does not draw that salary; for the moment the salary is not paid. However, occasion might demand at any time that a separate minister of defence production be appointed, and in that case I think every hon. member would wish him to receive the usual salary of $15,000 per annum. Through an error this ministry was not included in the salaries bill, and it is now proposed to correct that error.
The second section provides that the act, which would normally expire on July 31, 1956, will not expire and that the section providing for its expiry shall be repealed. As I explained when the resolution was under discussion, the reason for that is that the work of the department is a continuing work. Perhaps at earlier stages in the life of the department the work has not been as complicated and as difficult as it is at the moment. The department has under construction the mid-Canada early warning line, a large and important and difficult project located halfway between here and the Arctic

ocean. It also has under development a supersonic fighter plane involving a new supersonic engine and a new airframe. In addition it has all the supply problems incidental to maintaining troops in Germany and in Canada, and responsibility for keeping the equipment of the army, navy and air force up to the required standards.
Earlier discussion indicated that there is no particular objection to extending the life of the department. The necessity for extending its life is that it is impossible to hold the class of men we have in the department on the basis of temporary jobs. People who see that their jobs are going to expire in one year start looking for other jobs, and quite properly so. We know now that the services of these men and women will be required for a number of years, and we believe they are entitled to the security extended to service in permanent departments of government. Therefore it is proposed to make this department a permanent department.
The department has been permanent in effect since it was formed in 1939. After the department of munitions and supply was liquidated in 1948 its work was carried on as a branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce without a departmental act. It was found most difficult to carry on in that way, and we were glad indeed to have reason for forming the Department of Defence Production and asking parliament to enact a proper Defence Production Act.
Since 1939 the Department of Defence Production has spent probably $17 or $18 billion, yet it has been free from dishonesty, maladministration and the difficulties that frequently beset defence purchasing. I can tell hon. members from experience that defence purchasing is the most difficult type of purchasing to be undertaken by any government department.
The munitions and supply act was enacted in 1939, and was amended from time to time as the experience of the department indicated was necessary. The present act was based on the final edition of the munitions and supply act, and has proved to be comprehensive enough to cover all the situations we encounter in defence purchasing. It was drafted with that purpose in view and was based on the experience of several years of defence purchasing in wartime. We believe it is a model act.
I may tell hon. members that practically every country has the equivalent of our Defence Production Act. I am familiar with the acts in vogue in the United States and the United Kingdom, and I can say that the powers taken under our act are considerably
Defence Production Act more modest than those granted by either of the two acts I have mentioned.
There seems to be no objection to extending the life of the department; that appears to all hon. members as reasonable, but there was objection raised to extending the life of the Defence Production Act. During debate on the resolution I undertook to examine the situation with a view to amending the bill to take cognizance of some of the objections raised earlier. The matter has been gone into most thoroughly with the Department of Justice, with the Prime Minister and with the officials of my department, and for reasons which I shall state I cannot say at this time that we are prepared to amend the Defence Production Act in any manner whatsoever.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, May 24, consideration of the motion of Mr. Knowles for the second reading of Bill No. 379, to amend the Senate and House of Commons Act.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house will recall that in the short time I had available on the previous occasion when we discussed this bill, I pointed out that there were certain obvious inequalities-perhaps I could use that word- in the proposals that had been put before the house by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
I realize that the explanation he gave was an understandable one, namely that he thought the bill would be more acceptable in its present form than in some other form, though he probably would be prepared to say that the principle he was trying to have established by parliament was that a cabinet minister should not hold a directorship in a company during the time he was a member of the cabinet. For the reason one has not far to seek, of course. It is that there may be occasions when, at least in theory, a minister might be obliged to devote some time to the duties of a director, and that possibly the obligation of a cabinet minister is to devote his full time to being a minister of the crown.
This has not always been the case in Canada. I think everyone recognizes the fact that in late years it is true that the work of a cabinet minister has been taking more of one's time than it formerly did. I do not suppose it was very long ago that many ministers found it possible to discharge their obligations to the crown and their service to parliament in part of the time during the week, and could in fact engage in other personal occupations for part of the time. But
7, 1955
Senate and House of Commons Act in recent years, with parliament sitting from five to six months a year, with the greatly increased number of bills that come before parliament and the greatly expanded services that are being given to the public through the administration, a minister in many cases is rather wishful that the day had more than 24 hours, and there is not too much time to devote to personal affairs. Nevertheless, sir, until this debate arose I do not think the point was ever made that there should not be any time left for a minister to devote to other affairs to which he felt he owed an obligation, without for the moment examining whether such obligations may be such as to have a commanding demand on his time.
In the course of his introductory remarks the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre referred, as I recall it, to two countries outside Canada as examples, and I wish to deal briefly with his one reference to the United States and his one reference to the United Kingdom. In the case of the United States, as I understood him he had reference to the swearing in of cabinet ministers by the newly constituted Republican administration some three years ago. The house will recall that one of the cabinet ministers chosen by the President was obliged to divest himself of certain holdings in a corporation before he was acceptable to that particular committee of congress which passes on the acceptability of cabinet ministers.
That case is entirely different from that which is supposed to be placed before us in this bill. The objection taken at the time to the cabinet minister was not that he was a director of a corporation. The objection taken was that his holdings in a particular corporation were very substantial and that the corporation not only had many contracts with the government but in some cases exclusive contracts, especially in connection with the production of war materials and the like. It was not the case that he would have to devote some time to merely being a director, nor was there any suggestion that the trusteeship which he undertook as a cabinet minister could not be carried out properly under the circumstances, but merely that he himself was financially greatly interested in the company concerned, and that that was not a matter which ought to be passed over lightly by the committee investigating his qualifications.
May I point out what every member of the house of course knows, that the system in the United States is wholly different from that which obtains here. There the president is responsible to congress, it is true, in the sense that certain choices of personnel have to be approved by committees of congress in

Senate and House of Commons Act some cases, but he accepts full responsibility and indeed has visited on him the onus of full responsibility for the administration of the government of the United States.
That is not the situation here, sir. We as a cabinet are responsible both to one another and to the prime minister, and the cabinet as such is responsible to parliament in a wholly different manner from that which obtains south of the border. In any event, I stress the fact that to cite the instance of Mr. Wilson as an example of what has been done elsewhere which should be followed in Canada is merely to gloss over the great difference in the constitutional effect in both countries.
My hon. friend also mentioned, but only in one sentence, the practice in the United Kingdom. I was rather expecting him to give us some information about it, but perhaps because he felt his time was limited he did not pursue it further. He left with us the impression that the practice in the United Kingdom was such that if it were followed here we would in fact adopt the amendment to the Senate and House of Commons Act that he is proposing. 1 intend to make some reference to the practice in the United Kingdom, and to point out that it seems to me illogical to suggest amendment of the Senate and House of Commons Act as a way of carrying out what he apparently has in mind.
In the United Kingdom, as I think we are all aware, directorships are matters of emolument, and certainly in the past at any rate have been lucrative to those holding them. In Canada perhaps that is also true in some cases, but certainly not on the scale that has obtained in the past at least in the United Kingdom. I should also point out that in the United Kingdom they have a unitary state, and we would not have the situation I have already mentioned with respect to provincially incorporated companies or federally incorporated companies. For that reason, sir, it might be supposed that in the United Kingdom they would have already taken the step that has been recommended to us by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. In other words, where no distinction could be made one would have thought that if they felt there should be a statute they could have passed one, because anyone serving in the cabinet there could only hold a directorship in a United Kingdom corporation or a foreign corporation, and it would have been easy to lay down the rules in that way.
The fact that they have not done so has led me to suppose there may be some merit in not setting up a statutory bar to anyone serving as a cabinet minister and retaining


or carrying on some other activity outside that of government. But I propose to examine in detail the practice in the United Kingdom, because it seems to me that in one sense it commends itself to us as a standard of practice. On the other hand, it definitely does lay down the rules which in effect obtain in this country in one form or another.
If I may have the permission of the house I should like to read from Hansard of the United Kingdom the rules that obtain there, for the purpose of placing them on the record and examining them to see if they are applicable to Canadian conditions. They will be found in Hansard of the 25 th of February, 1952, at pages 701 and 702. A statement was made by the then prime minister in answer to a question which apparently had been put to the ministry some time before. The question was:
What regulations govern the continuation of salaried service with a private company on appointment to ministerial office?
Perhaps hon. members would bear in mind that this happened just a few months after the government had changed in the fall of 1951, I think. The regulations are rather lengthy and I will have to crave the indulgence of the house for the purpose of examining them. I propose to read the record and then make some comments. The Prime Minister answered by asking leave to circulate a copy in the official report, which I take it is equivalent to asking that the document be incorporated in Hansard and not read. There are, as a matter of fact, eight rules. I shall read them from beginning to end and then, as I say, I should like to have the privilege of going back to discuss them. They are:
1.	It is a principle of public life that ministers must so order their affairs that no conflict arises, or appears to arise, between their private interests and their public duties.
2.	Such a conflict may arise if a minister takes an active part in any undertaking which may have contractual or other relations with a government department, more particularly with his own department. It may arise, not only if the minister has a financial interest in such an undertaking, but also if he is actively associated with any body, even of a philanthropic character, which might have negotiations or other dealings with the government or be involved in disputes with it. Furthermore, ministers should be free to give full attention to their official duties, and they should not engage in other activities which might be thought to distract their attention from those duties.
3.	Each minister must decide for himself how these principles apply to him. Over much of the field, as is shown below, there are established precedents; but in any case of doubt the prime minister of the day must be the final judge, and ministers should submit any such case to him for his direction.
4.	Where it is proper for a minister to retain any private interests, it is the rule that he should

declare that Interest to his colleagues if they have to discuss public business in any way affecting it, and that he should entirely detach himself from the consideration of that business.
5.	Ministers include all members of the government except unpaid assistant government whips.
6.	Ministers must on assuming office resign any directorships which they may hold, whether in public or in private companies and whether the directorship carries remuneration or is honorary. The only exception to this rule is that directorships in private companies established for the maintenance of private family estates, and only incidentally concerned in trading, may be retained subject to this reservation-that if at any time the minister feels that conflict is likely to arise between this private interest and his public duty, he should even in those cases divest himself of his directorship. Directorships or offices held in connection with philanthropic undertakings should also be resigned if there is any risk of conflict arising between the interests of the undertakings and the government.
7.	Ministers cannot be expected, on assuming office, to dispose of all their investments. But if a minister holds a controlling interest in any company considerations arise which are not unlike those governing the holding of directorships and, if there is any danger of a conflict of interest, the right course is for the minister to divest himself of his controlling interest in the company. There may also be exceptional cases where, even though no controlling interest is involved, the actual holdings of particular shares in concerns closely associated with a minister's own department may create the danger of a conflict of interest. Where a minister considers this to be the case, he should divest himself of the holding.
8.	Ministers should scrupulously avoid speculative investments in securities about which they have, or may be thought to have, earlier or confidential information likely to affect the price of those securities.
I notice that there was no debate on that answer, and presumably it was accepted by the house as a general statement that would be applied by the then prime minister in any future change in connection with his ministry. Presumably also he had applied those rules in the formation of the ministry which had occurred perhaps three or four months before that.
So far as I have been able to ascertain, sir, those are the only published rules of any kind with respect to the problem with which we are now dealing. There may be others in other jurisdictions, and perhaps hon. members will be able to correct me, but so far as I have been able to determine there are no other rules. However, as I may have implied a few moments ago, there are certain practices in the United States, and I have no doubt there may be some obscure statutes there that are the authority whereby the respective congressional committees consider the qualifications of the various candidates who are recommended for appointment by the president.
I should like to point out to the house that these are the rules which Mr. Churchill laid down, and which presumably he applied,
Senate and House of Commons Act and in the course of which he made the frank statement that with respect to certain matters therein it was for the minister himself to decide whether or not he was affected by these particular rules. He also went on to say that in the final result it would be for the prime minister to make the decision as to whether or not the minister should divest himself of these particular interests.
On the matter of interests, sir, may I repeat what the hon. member said to me in the few minutes I had two weeks ago, that he was not making any suggestion that in the particular case he had in mind and to which he referred there was any conflict of interest; that there was any financial advantage, or indeed that there was anything more than this proposal which had always been in his mind. Perhaps it could be said that certain present circumstances would only add to the strength of his argument. He did not, however, assert anything which in my view would contravene the spirit of these rules. In other words he did not make an argument for the amendment he was proposing which would be borne out by conduct which the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom was suggesting was improper under the circumstances.
I therefore repeat, Mr. Speaker, that it would seem to me that until recent years at least there has been no settled practice in commonwealth countries-perhaps in others for all I know-of a growing restriction on the activities of cabinet ministers outside the administration of their departments and in common with their colleagues in the administration of the government. If there is or has been a tendency to restrict those activities, it has grown up just in recent years, probably for the reason I have given, that it would seem there was not enough time in a day to devote to anything else but the affairs of the public.
I realize that some of the rules I have just read are more or less a repetition of rules which had been stated by a former prime minister of the United Kingdom many years ago in connection with another incident. Presumably in the 40-odd years that have elapsed these rules have been observed by succeeding prime ministers, and for some time at least these rules have been merely a reflection of a long-standing practice there. However, I think it is fair to say that I do not recall, nor can I find very much record in the United Kingdom of anyone suggesting prior to this, that a person should not be a cabinet minister if he was the director of a corporation, and this probably breaks new ground in that respect. I repeat that perhaps other researchers may find an earlier record of it.
4506	HOUSE OF
Senate and House of Commons Act
For these reasons, therefore, I suggest that the bill before us, even if it were considered to be progressive, is at least no more than timely. It is perhaps even a little before its time. Evidently public opinion in the commonwealth countries, and perhaps in others, has not up until very recently at any rate approached this problem with any particular concern about whether cabinet ministers should or should not be directors of companies. I grant you, sir, that I have not found it possible to search all the statutes of other commonwealth countries and, as I say, there may be exceptions that I have not been able to find.
To go back over the rules, therefore, may I point out that the standard of conduct expected of cabinet ministers seems to include, first of all of course-and so obviously is it the case that it was left to the end to state it-that they should not engage in speculative investments in securities about which they have or might be thought to have confidential or early information.
That is, as I have intimated, a throwback to an incident in the United Kingdom of 40-odd years ago; and I do not recall any such incident in Canadian public life, though there may have been one. In fact, my recollection is that even prime ministers in this country have held directorships in companies, though not in recent years. We haye gradually approached this problem as one which rests on public opinion, because the prime minister of the day is obliged to make his choice of cabinet ministers acceptable to the public, and acceptable of course to parliament as well, though not in the sense that the president of the United States must choose cabinet ministers who are acceptable to congress. I fear many of us would not be on the front benches if we had to submit our qualifications to opposition members.
Let us therefore consider these rules, though not in detail, because I do not propose to take them in detail. However, they divide themselves into three general groups. First there is the matter of private interest. And with respect to that, as I have said I do not find any evidence of any suggestion that private interest is conflicting in any way with public duty. I do not wish to widen the subject of the discussion, but my understanding is that hardly anyone would expect a cabinet minister so to remove himself from the trade and commerce of the country that he would not be able to resume his occupation or his livelihood should he cease to be a cabinet minister. All that need be said on that point is that


his private interest should not conflict with his public duties. We are in complete agreement with that, of course.
The next rule has to do with the holding of directorships. Once again we find that in this particular case there is an exception with respect to private companies for the maintenance of family estates and only incidentally concerned in trading. From the wording it must be clear that the Prime Minister had in mind trading as such, that is, companies doing business by way of contracts with the government and so on. We had again here the inference of private profit, or the conflict of private interest with public duty.
In this case I pause only long enough to say that the sponsor of this bill is not suggesting that we are discussing that point at the moment.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

Is it not correct that the
Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, before he stated the exception, laid down a general rule against cabinet ministers holding directorships?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext:
What he said was this:
Ministers must, on assuming office, resign any directorships which they may hold, whether in public or in private companies, and whether the directorship carries remuneration or is honorary.
Then he went on with the exception. The exception is the one I have indicated, that he was not to be concerned in trading as such- a company dealing with the government by way of contract, and for profit. For a moment, if my hon. friend wishes, I shall comment on the general statement rather than the exception. The general statement was that a minister must resign certain directorships upon assuming office. My hon. friend made the point, however, in the course of his argument, that we are discussing generally the course to be adopted in Canada.
A full explanation has been made of the practice heretofore obtaining in Canada, namely that a total disclosure has been made, at least in recent years, to the prime minister of the day, as to the holding of certain offices in corporations. The prime minister, having been made aware of this, concluded that this was a matter which rested with the minister concerned. I am now referring to the occasion the Prime Minister referred to when he accepted office in 1941. That having been the practice heretofore, it might therefore appear that the proposal of the hon. member would be one that would apply in the future to any newly sworn-in ministers of the crown.
I take it that in this particular case Mr. Churchill was saying that. I do not know

that he did in fact take into his ministry prior to that date anyone who at that date had been a director of a corporation. I have not made inquiries; but it would seem that on this particular date he proposed that hereafter any minister he asked to serve with him would be expected to resign his directorships. I have no way of knowing whether in fact that has been done from that date to this, but I suppose it has. I address myself to the fact that it would seem that the plain statement in the preliminary sentence was qualified by the remainder of the section I have read.
Now, with respect to shareholdings, I do not need to go into that because the hon. member does not cover it in his bill. However, I have read the whole of it so there will not be any suggestion that we confine ourselves for the moment solely to the purpose of the amendment before the house. Because I think the problem is much greater than just the immediate question of whether the Senate and House of Commons Act should be amended so that from the date the amendment was passed by the house those of us sitting here who happened to be directors would have to divest ourselves of those directorships, and that thereafter the prime minister would be put in the position that in offering a post to one who appeared to him likely to serve the public well in that post he should always make sure, before he was sworn in, that he had resigned any directorship or other office he might hold in private life.
That brings me, therefore, to the problem which confronts us in determining what should be done with regard to the bill before the house. The bill does propose, as I said the other day, that there would be certain exceptions to the rule that would be established with respect to cabinet ministers. A minister could not perform the duties of his office if he were a director of a corporation incorporated by federal statute or by letters patent issued by the crown. That would leave it, sir, that other ministers might serve and at the same time hold directorships in provincially incorporated companies.
, I know the hon. member hastened to say that if I would move an amendment to the bill he would be glad to adopt the suggestion that cabinet ministers should not hold any of these offices; but I think it points up the peculiar position we have in this country, namely that we are not a unitary state and that possibly our ministers should not be subject to rules which were laid down in another jurisdiction which happens to be a unitary state. Nor should it be supposed, sir, that our position is precisely that of the
Senate and House of Commons Act United States, where they have other practices and other constitutional obligations.
For this reason it seems to me that we ought to examine the problem a little more than the mere discussion of it as the principle of this bill would allow; and that we should not as a parliament impose a bar against a future prime minister without very carefully considering what the difficulties might be, in so far as we can see them, which might be attached to the formation of a ministry at some time in the future.
It seems therefore, sir, that it would be better-and I place this before the hon. member knowing that he holds strong views on it-to say that this is not just a simple bill of six or seven lines that could be passed in this house in the course of the next two or three weeks or even a month. There are matters that ought to be considered at greater length than it is possible for us to do at the present time. We might do one of two things, sir. We might withdraw the bill for the moment on the assumption, and indeed on the assurance, that it will be given full consideration in the interval between now and the next session of parliament; or alternatively, we might consider it in this house in a committee.
I realize that what I have said might indicate that I would personally agree, after consideration, to an amendment to the statute. I hope that is not taken from what I have said, because as at present advised it seems to me unwise to have a statutory bar. Nevertheless it is not unwise, in my view, to consider rules that might be stated in much the same manner that Mr. Churchill stated rules in the United Kingdom for his guidance in the formation of a ministry. Let us however admit that if these rules were stated in the manner that Mr. Churchill laid down, they would not be binding on any subsequent prime minister, who would accept responsibility to parliament and to the country for any deviation that he might feel ih honour bound to make from those rules. Perhaps that is what the hon. member has in mind.
There has been a quite steady approach to this problem, with a definite withdrawal of cabinet ministers over the years from private activity, and in time no doubt the number who will take part in other private affairs will be very small, as in fact it is at the moment. Nevertheless, even then the hon. member might feel that there ought to be a statutory provision with respect to the holding of these various offices.
I think I have made it clear-I hope I have-that I am not convinced there ought to be such a statutory bar, nor am I to be

Senate and House of Commons Act taken as saying that we ought to go back to the old days when many ministers did in fact hold directorships in companies, or that they should be allowed by practice and indulgence to devote considerable time to their private affairs. A parliamentary session today is lengthy. The preparation for it is onerous, and the discharge of administrative duties, even when parliament is not sitting, certainly takes a great deal of the minister's time. I firmly believe also that if a minister is not sitting in parliament or discharging the duties of his office or preparing for the next session of parliament, it is his obligation to defend the administration of which he is a member in public, and to see the public as often as he can so he may be aware of public sentiment on any given point and be prepared for it at the coming session of parliament. That does take a very great deal of one's time; but that is not to say that the holding of directorships in itself is wrong or improper. Indeed, no one has suggested that so far in speaking on this particular bill.
If my hon. friend does not feel that he can let this matter stand for the time being I propose to move:
That this bill be not now read a second time, but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on privileges and elections.
You might ask me, Mr. Chairman, why privileges and elections? There is no particular privilege of a member of parliament involved here; but as I think hon. members know we have always-at least I personally have always-taken the view that the standing committees of the house can be most useful, and that names themselves do not mean very much. If we could refer more matters to committees than we have been doing in the past we would have better legislation and indeed better consideration of the subjects we choose to bring before this house. It seems to me that these rules- and, as I have said, the statutes of the United States congress and any rules or obligations that may be imposed in other jurisdictions- are matters which could be given serious consideration by the committee.
While I do not suppose they would feel that they could improve on some of these, representations ought to be made before the committee with respect to any variation there might be under Canadian conditions which would make these rules, if not inapplicable, at least inappropriate for our people here.
I was rather interested, sir, to find that in fact this seemed to be the only declaration made by a commonwealth prime minister since that which had been made by Mr. Asquith on another occasion before the first


world war. If there has been any other declaration of principles as a whole rather than merely an explanation of a detached incident it would be desirable to have it to guide this parliament in determining its course in the circumstances. Whether the committee could in fact recommend to parliament rules which could be incorporated in the Senate and House of Commons Act is a matter of opinion.
As I said a moment ago, I am not yet convinced that there ought to be a statutory provision for this; and if I were convinced I think it would be with the conviction that we could only have a short statement, perhaps of a minimal nature, which would permit a future prime minister to have as much leeway as possible in the formation of his ministry.

I believe this is something that must be established by the Prime Minister. There is a vast difference between the government in Canada and the government in the United States. The Minister of Finance has indicated that there is a greater degree of obligation upon a minister in the United States to divest himself of any possible conflict of interests. Senate and House of Commons Act answerable day by day to the house. The situation here is quite different. Our tradition is parallel to the tradition in the United Kingdom, as has been clearly indicated by the minister himself.
There is a long tradition in relation to this matter, and it goes back much earlier than the minister mentioned. As an example, in 1906 Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman laid down a rule for the conduct of ministers, and I should like to quote just one statement. Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman said that all directorships held by ministers must be resigned except in the case of honorary directorships in connection with philanthropic undertakings and directorships in private companies. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the debate was interrupted I had dealt with two sections of the bill and was about to deal with the objections to the Defence Production Act which were raised when the resolution preceding the bill was under discussion. I shall now proceed with the latter question.
I should like to deal first with the statement I made in March, 1951, on the nature of the special powers contained in the Defence Production Act. Reference to the continuing nature of those powers should not be taken out of its context but should be read in conjunction with statements on the situation made at that time. We were confronted with what we then believed to be an extraordinary situation, one we hoped would clear up within the three-year period set for the defence program. Our hopes have not been fulfilled. For the better part of four years we have been living in what was once considered an extraordinary situation, and there is still no indication of when we can expect it to improve to the point where our defence production program can be cut back. The statement I made in 1951 was made in good faith, in the earnest hope that we would now be living in a world in which normal peacetime conditions would prevail. Such is not the case, and it is in the light of present-day circumstances that I am compelled to recommend the continuation of the Defence Production Act in its present form.
At the resolution stage the Leader of the Opposition implied that in asking for the continuation of the Defence Production Act the government is getting away from traditional methods of parliamentary procedure and parliamentary responsibility, and that there is a denial of the supremacy of parliament and the rule of law. I must admit that I am only a layman in this field, but it seems to me that this is not the case. Under our present parliamentary procedures the house has an opportunity to review the responsibilities and functions of each department at least once a year, when the estimates

are being considered. Traditionally this is the way in which legislation can be examined critically, the way in which it can be determined whether or not it meets the needs and conditions of the times.
Furthermore, in setting up a department of defence production, the minister in charge of that department is fully responsible to parliament for the way in which he discharges his responsibilities and for the department's operations. At any time he can be called upon by this house to account for his actions. Surely this is parliamentary procedure and parliamentary responsibility. As for the rule of law, there are numerous references to the right of appeal to the courts against the crown under this act. I would draw the attention of hon. members to section 37 which, while it does not permit court action against an investigator or controller in the performance of his duties, goes on to state that "nothing in this section limits or restricts the rights of any person against the crown."
To sum up the points I have been making, there is nothing in the act that denies the supremacy of parliament, nor is there anything that prevents recourse to a court of law or that contravenes the jurisdiction of the courts.
Before the resolution on the present bill was concurred in on March 14, I gave an undertaking that the government would consider the request made by the hon. members for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) and Peace River (Mr. Low). This request was to include in the act a clause which would make the powers of the department subject to review within a reasonable period.
This question was referred to the Department of Justice, and officers of that department pointed out that in view of the fact that a review of legislation is a matter which parliament can undertake at any time, an express provision requiring a periodic review of this kind would have no real significance. In order to require a review by parliament and attach to it legal consequences it would be necessary, for example, to provide that the act would expire at a stated time unless reviewed and reapproved or re-enacted before the expiration of that time. This obviously was not the intent indicated by the request put forward by the hon. members.
Suggestions of the Department of Justice to achieve the results desired by the hon. members were along these lines, as in each case they required that certain sections of the act be singled out at this time and
Defence Production Act designated as clauses which should expire at a given date in the future. Again this is not satisfactory, as it is impossible to separate the powers of the act in this way. I would point out again that this act was drawn up on the basis of experience gained in handling defence production over a period of years, a period that included the unsettled era following world war II as well as the years of actual war. In my opinion these are the powers needed to carry out Canada's defence production program. Either you have a defence production act with these powers, and all these powers, or you have no act at all.
Much has been made of the so-called extraordinary powers in the Defence Production Act. Hon. members have been urged from several parts of the house to read the act carefully. I agree that this should be done, but I wonder whether some of those who have made the plea have followed their own advice and have read all the sections with equal care. There is not the slightest suggestion in the act that personal liberties or freedoms can be menaced or abridged in any way. There is in the act, and I think there should continue to be, authority to interfere with property rights in appropriate cases.
My hon. friends opposite have not seen fit to bring to the attention of the house the safeguards which are also contained in the act. Stirring denunciations have been made of sections 23 and 24, relating to directed contracts and requisitioning of supplies, but no mention has been made of section 25, which clearly provides for compensation to be paid, such compensation to be arrived at by mutual agreement or, in default of such agreement, to be fixed by the exchequer court. In other words this is definitely not confiscation nor anything approaching confiscation. It is in fact no different from the Expropriation Act which has been in force since confederation, and longer if we go back to English law. Under the Expropriation Act the land is first expropriated by the crown and compensation is worked out afterward. As I have already pointed out, this is similar to the procedure under the Defence Production Act.
A good deal has been said about section 32, dealing with offences, but no mention has been made of section 33, dealing with the defence of due diligence which may be made by any person charged with an offence. This clause gives the person who has been charged an opportunity to establish that he exercised all due diligence to comply with the terms of the act but failed because of reasons

Defence Production Act beyond his control. In addition, nothing in the act prevents any person who feels himself aggrieved from having recourse to the courts.
Now let me turn for a moment to sections 26, 27, 28 and 29, all of which have been mentioned adversely. I cannot see how it would be possible to have an act dealing with defence procurement and production without section 26, which deals with priorities. Priorities regulations are still in effect today in the United States. With respect to section 27, I do not feel that it is any indictment of this section, which deals with the appointment of a controller, to point out that it has not been used since 1951. What is important is not whether it has been used but whether it is a power which might be necessary, and what the consequences would be if it -were deleted. Using this criterion, I feel that this is a necessary part of the whole purpose of the act.
With respect to section 28, dealing with relief from obligations imposed by the act, I would point out two things. First, this is a power exercised not by the minister but by the governor in council. Second, it is intended to help, not to penalize. In other words it is a necessary adjunct to the earlier powers contained in the act, and is designed to protect any business firms which might otherwise get into trouble through entering into a defence contract or complying with an order or regulation. The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) asked if this section had been invoked during the life of this act, and the answer is no.
With regard to section 29, which deals with the appointment of an investigator and which has not been used since this act came into force, I should only like to say that this is a protection on which I believe the country is entitled to insist when the whole security of the state and the lives of its citizens may depend on matters being thoroughly, properly and expeditiously investigated. Furthermore, this section does not confer on the investigator any powers over and above those contained in the Inquiries Act, nor are the powers of entry and seizure any greater than those of the Income Tax Act. I am sure hon. members will agree that neither of these acts is as vital to the safety of the nation as is the act under consideration.
In the debate on the resolution I was asked the number of prosecutions under section 32, and the date of the last one. There have been nine different cases since the act came into force. The date of the last conviction was May 30, 1953.
I would ask hon. members to consider carefully what it is we are discussing today.

No one likes the idea of large armed services, large expenditures for what are essentially unproductive and destructive purposes, and life in a world threatened by war waged with weapons of almost unbelievable powers of destruction. Nevertheless such are the facts of life. In addition, we do not now enjoy the leisure and time granted to earlier generations in dealing with threats to peace. When we act we have to act quickly. I do not know how the impression has been gained that all is now well, and that our difficulties are behind us. Certainly we have found no such happy interlude in defence production matters. We are faced with difficult and challenging duties which we hope to discharge conscientiously and expeditiously. These duties relate to the safety and security of each one of us, and I should not like to accept the responsibility for recommending that the means by which these tasks are carried out should now be made less efficient.
In conclusion I may say that I think I can claim to have more experience in defence purchasing than any other man now living. At least I am the only man doing defence purchasing today who did the same job throughout the last great war. I have tried to carry out defence purchasing under the munitions and supply act, then without an act, and now under the Defence Production Act. I say to this house that it is my conviction that to carry out an efficient job of defence procurement the department must be armed with an act giving the powers necessary to do the job.
I have had a great deal of experience in buying for governments. I started some 40 years ago as a consulting engineer, and I have been doing some buying for governments ever since. I can tell this house that generally speaking a government order does not receive the same attention as a privately placed order. The reason is that generally speaking the government cannot put on as much pressure as does the private buyer. That has been my experience, and that was my experience in buying for our defence procurement during the years when I had no act to support me.
I believe that when this country is supplying great sums for defence it is entitled to the assurance that those funds are being spent efficiently and carefully. For that reason I tell this house that as a minister of the crown I cannot conscientiously recommend that my department be deprived of powers which I believe are essential to that purpose. I may also say that I do not intend to make any such recommendation.

Well, sir, I am not one of those who attach very much importance to cries of that kind, because in my reading I have learned that the same thing was said 50 years ago about the same two parties. But, sir, to those who give ear to that kind of talk let me make it abundantly clear now that in this situation there is as between the government on the one hand and us of Her Majesty's loyal opposition on the other a deep issue, a clear-cut issue, an issue as to the status and the authority as well as the prestige of the parliament of Canada; and on that issue, that clear-cut, deep issue we are prepared to fight. We are not unmindful of the fact that this is an advanced stage of this session, that we have had a taste within the past two days of a temperature of 90 degrees, but here is a case that we consider to be of the highest importance, one that lays on every member of this house the highest kind of responsibility; and on this issue we now join battle.
Sir, the bill, as the minister reminded us this afternoon in seductive tones, is very brief. We are asked to measure the importance of this bill by its brevity. Well, sir, there are only two short provisions in it. I do not know that we have had any shorter bill before this house in a long time. It is quite unlikely that we shall have as short a bill as this is before us again for a long time. But let no hon. member of this house misjudge the importance and significance of this bill simply because of its unusual brevity. This bill, both in its effect and in the principle involved, is of far-reaching importance and of the utmost significance.
I can dismiss very briefly, sir, the provision in the bill that proposes an increase in the salary of the Minister of Defence Production from $10,000 to $15,000 per annum. Of course this was an oversight when the amendment to the Salaries Act was passed just over a year ago. It seems to me it should not be introduced in a bill of this kind; it ought to be handled by way of an amendment to the
Defence Production Act Salaries Act, but we are not making an issue of that. So far as that provision in the bill is concerned we shall put no opposition in its way.
But, sir, let no hon. member of this house dismiss, minimize or overlook the importance of eight words contained in this bill. These words are;
Section 41 of the said act is repealed.
There are only a few words. Should we be spending time on so few words in this House of Commons at an advanced stage of the session, when most are impatient to conclude the business of the house as quickly as possible? Sir, the significance of these words is this. The measure we are asked to pass tonight is more far-reaching than the original bill that was passed in 1951. There is this fundamental difference in the two bills. The bill of 1951 was a bill which under the extraordinary circumstances then obtaining vested extraordinary powers in the government and in the minister, but it made it all subject to a time limit, which made it necessary for the government to come back to parliament if they wanted an extension of the life of that measure and of those powers, within the space of five years. But what are we asked to legislate for here tonight? Sir, we are asked in effect to re-enact this entire measure, and to remove from it that one saving provision.
Therefore, sir, what we have before us tonight is something much more than simply the continuation of a measure. The act of 1951 had a limitation of time. This amendment, if passed, will create an act without any limitation of time or limitation of any other sort by way of substitute. That is the true basis of comparison. That is the true measure of the effect of the legislation now before us.
Sir, I ask again, as I asked at the resolution stage, that no hon. member of this house should cast his vote on this amending bill until he has gone back and read the 22 pages of the act which, by these mere eight words, we are asked to extend and to embed on a permanent basis in the statute law of this country.
It is clear that we should turn back our thoughts to four years ago, to the conditions under which and the state of mind in which parliament considered and passed the Defence Production Act.
What were those conditions? Sir, it was nine months after the outbreak of hostilities in Korea, when the forces of aggression had swept over the 38th parallel and had overrun almost all of southern Korea; when the United Nations, taking advantage of the fortunate absence of Russia from the security council, had passed resolutions condemning

Defence Production Act that act of aggression and summoning the member nations to render aid in resisting aggression; and when Canada, along with 15 other nations, responded by sending aid in the form of army, air force and navy contributions to the forces of the United Nations. Then when, as it seemed, victory had been snatched from defeat, we found Chinese troops pouring over the Yalu river by the hundreds of thousands. It appeared that a desperate defeat was about to be inflicted upon the forces of the United Nations, and for a time a debacle was barely avoided.
These, let me remind hon. members, were the facts that stared this House of Commons in the face four years ago when in March, 1951, we were asked under those extraordinary and critical conditions to pass legislation that was itself of an extraordinary nature.
Sir, extensive description is really not necessary because the Prime Minister himself, at the resolution stage just three months ago, used these words to describe the situation with which we were confronted, along with the other nations of the free world, in April, 1951. These were his words, as we find them at page 1904 of Hansard of March 10, 1955:
Hon. members will recall that when the Department of Defence Production was established on April 1, 1951, it was to meet an emergency situation brought to a head by the fighting in Korea.

Sir, those were the conditions according to the Prime Minister's admission. This bill was passed to meet an emergency situation brought to a head by the fighting in Korea. Those were days of scarcities of materials, of a world-wide scramble for strategic materials. It was a world caught unawares by aggression, when it seemed that we were on the verge, it might well be, of a third world war. I can remember one of the colleagues of the Minister of Defence Production coming into the opposition lobby at that time and telling us in grave tones, with a long face, that it looked to him as though we were on the verge of a third world war.
That was the condition under which this statute was born. That was the frame of mind the government asked on the part of

parliament in approaching this matter. That was the very time when parliament at the request of the government was legislating, if you please, in terms like these, and I read from the preamble of the Emergency Powers Act which received royal assent on March 21, 1951:
Whereas an international emergency exists that threatens the security of Canada:
And whereas it is essential that emergency powers be conferred to enable measures to be taken as urgently required from time to time to carry out adequate defence preparations, to regulate the economy of Canada to meet the needs of defence and to stabilize the economy and to safeguard it from disruption that may result from defence preparations in Canada or from emergency measures taken in other countries, in order that defence preparations may not be impeded;
That was the kind of legislation that parliament was passing in March, 1951, at the request of the government. Parliament was legislating in terms to give parliamentary and statutory acknowledgment to the fact that a grave international emergency existed that threatened the security of Canada.
Let us then compare those conditions with conditions in the world today. The Minister of Defence Production has asked parliament and the country in effect to say that there is no material change in conditions as between March, 1951, and today. What then is the meaning of the statements we have heard in Canada from the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) about the improvement in conditions? In fairness it must be said that they have been guarded statements, as properly they should be. Nobody can say that there is no danger in the world today, but at any rate the Secretary of State for External Affairs has permitted us to believe that there has been improvement. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has invited us to believe that there has been improvement. Mr. Dulles has said that there has been improvement. Sir Anthony Eden has said, not once but on various occasions, that the situation is improving.
Are we to cast aside all these reliable assertions and accept the position which the Minister of Defence Production puts before us in saying that there is no material improvement, that to all intents and purposes the situation is as bad as it was in 1951 and therefore we should give him all the powers that were considered necessary in March, 1951, when parliament gave recognition to the existence of an international emergency which threatened the security of Canada?
Has there been no improvement since March, 1955? At the time this measure was being discussed at the resolution stage all the interested countries had not ratified the treaty

for the rearmament of Germany, but we know now that this has been accomplished in the meantime, and that the time has now come which has been looked forward to for a long time, when the western nations are in the position, according to the accepted phrase, of being "able to negotiate from strength". Although four years ago we were faced with an international emergency threatening the security of Canada; although we have now, four years later, reached the position where the western nations feel that they are able to negotiate from strength, the Minister of Defence Production says there is no change in the situation which would justify parliament in subtracting from him one iota of those sweeping powers he had voted to him in 1951 at the hands of parliament.
So that this debate may be cast in its proper perspective, let me state with care the position we take. The minister correctly said this afternoon that we do not question the necessity for the continuation of the Department of Defence Production. The case for the continuation of that department was established to our satisfaction even before the resolution was introduced.
We agree that the civil servants in the employ of this department should not be on a mere temporary basis. We agree that a department of this kind should be able under present conditions to handle the problems of procurement better than a crown agency like the Canadian Commercial Corporation. So we support unreservedly the position that the *department should be made permanent and that those who now have temporary status should enjoy the same status as the employees of other departments.
Second, we are quite prepared, as we said at the resolution stage of this measure, that the department should be given adequate powers to meet any foreseeable needs having regard to the situation and having regard to the fact that parliament is going to continue to meet and is not, we trust, going to be sent home indefinitely. But we say, and we say with all conviction, that the powers in this bill are excessive, and that under present conditions there can be no justification for the government asking that these sweeping, yes, untrammelled powers, be vested in the government and in the minister, since so many are vested directly in the minister.
We say that it is a curious paradox, indeed a paradox that could exist only at the hands and in the minds of this government, that when the world was faced with such an international emergency as to threaten the security of Canada the government asked parliament to confer such powers upon the government subject to a time limit, but now when the
Defence Production Act western world describes itself as being in a position to negotiate from strength, when the situation according to the description of every responsible world leader has improved substantially, the government opposite asks parliament to go further than it did in 1951 and confer these powers afresh, but this time without the effective limitation in time that was proposed and accepted in 1951.

Is the house going to legislate on that basis? Is the house going to go so far beyond the measures it took under those conditions and in the face of that statement by the government in 1951, and enact today a more far-reaching measure than the one it enacted in 1951?
In his speech tonight the minister sought to play down the provisions of this measure. To listen to him, Mr. Speaker, one would have thought it was such a milk and water measure that it did not give him adequate powers for the task that has been assigned to him. I hope the house will not be misled by these cooing, seductive words of the Minister of Defence Production tonight into thinking that these powers are not what in fact they are. Look at some of these provisions, Mr. Speaker.
Section 15 reads as follows:
15. The minister may, on behalf of Her Majesty and subject to the provisions of this act-
You will note, Mr. Speaker, that it is the minister who may do these things; it is not the governor in council. These are powers conferred directly on the minister.

Then, sir, we find that section 31 says:
The governor In council may do and authorize such acts and things and make from time to time such orders and regulations as he deems necessary to control and regulate the production, processing, distribution, acquisition, disposition or use of essential materials or the supply or use of essential services for the purposes of
