(b)	ensuring that abnormal requirements of essential materials and services for defence supplies or defence projects are obtained in the manner least likely to cause disruption of the trade and commerce of Canada dependent on those materials and services, which disruption might impede or prejudice the defence preparations or the economic stability of Canada.

Then, sir, it goes on:
Subject to the regulations, if any, the minister may, by order, as he deems necessary for the purposes specified in subsection (1),
(a)	require any person who produces, possesses, deals in or has in his possession or control any essential materials to deal with, supply or dispose of any such materials in such manner and in such priority to that person's other transactions as the minister may prescribe;
(b)	require any person who produces or processes any essential materials to produce or process any such materials in such manner and in such priority to that person's other production or processing operations as the minister may prescribe;
(c)	prescribe the quantities of, the manner and circumstances in which and the conditions on which any essential materials may be produced, processed, used, acquired or disposed of, either generally or within periods of time prescribed by the minister, and for these purposes may require persons to obtain permits;
(d)	require any person who supplies any essential service to supply the service to such persons, to such extent and on such conditions as the minister may prescribe;
(e)	prescribe the restrictions and conditions according to which an essential service may be supplied or used, either generally or within periods of time prescribed by the minister, and for these purposes may require persons to obtain permits;
(f)	fix the maximum prices, either by determining the selling price or the mark-up, at which and the terms and conditions on which any essential materials or essential services may be sold or offered for sale by any person; and require any seller to refund to any buyer any sum or consideration received in excess of a maximum selling price so fixed;
(g)	prescribe the circumstances in which and the terms and conditions on which, for any purposes of this act, permits shall be obtained from the minister or from a person designated by the minister; grant general or other permits; and amend, suspend or cancel any permit;
(h)	require any person to furnish such information respecting essential materials produced, processed or dealt in by him or essential services supplied by him, or respecting his production and other facilities relating thereto, in such time and manner as the minister may prescribe; and
(i)	do such further things in regard to the production, supply, distribution, and use of essential materials or essential services as may be authorized by order or regulation of the governor in council.
Section 32 goes on then to attach a penalty to a breach of the provisions of this act or of orders or regulations made under authority of this act, and these penalties may go up to two years' imprisonment or fines up to $5,000. That is what that act does, and those are the powers the act confers, some of them on the cabinet but many of them directly upon the Minister of Defence Production. Is it any wonder, sir, that the Prime Minister acknowledged in 1951 that no wider powers than these would be required in respect of defence procurement or defence production in the event of a third world war? These are the powers that made, were intended to make, and which the government now asks this house to grant to make the cabinet and minister omnipotent.
Defence Production Act
The minister made the amazing statement this evening that this bill goes no farther than the provisions of the comparable legislation in the United Kingdom. I do not know what on earth he was referring to. He must have a different kind of statute book of the United Kingdom to refer to from the one which I have been reading. The legislation that was passed in the United Kingdom in 1951, on the basis of the emergency arising out of aggression in Korea, does not hold a candle to this Defence Production Act of ours. The legislation that was enacted at Westminster in 1951 was entitled the Supplies and Services (Defence Purposes) Act, 1951. This received the royal assent on May 26, 1951. It simply added to the purposes for which certain powers were conferred on the cabinet by the Supplies and Services (Transitional Powers) Act, 1945, the following:
(a)	providing or securing supplies and services required for the defence of any part of His Majesty's dominions or any territory under His Majesty's protection or in which he has jurisdiction, or for the maintenance or restoration of peace and security in any part of the world, or for any measures arising out of a breach or apprehended breach of peace in any part of the world; and
(b)	preventing supplies or services being disposed of in a manner prejudicial to the defence of any part of His Majesty's dominions or any such territory as aforesaid or to peace and security in any part of the world or to any such measures as aforesaid;
Then it went on to attach safeguards even to the use of those powers, which are very much more limited than the powers contained in our Defence Production Act, If you refer back to the act of 1945, the Supplies and Services (Transitional Powers) Act, chapter 10, which was amended by the statute to which I have just referred, it will be seen that the powers that were conferred even at the close of world war II were not as great. I ask hon. members to bear that in mind. Here I am referring to powers that were conferred upon the cabinet in Great Britain in December, 1945, just after the conclusion of hostilities and while conditions were still very disturbed. This act conferred certain powers upon the cabinet, not upon a minister. Section 1 provides:
If it appears to His Majesty to be necessary or expedient that any defence regulation to which this section applies should have effect for the purpose of so maintaining, controlling and regulating supplies and services as-
(a)	to secure a sufficiency of those essential to the wellbeing of the community or their equitable distribution or their availability at fair prices; or
(b)	to facilitate the demobilization and resettlement of persons and to secure the orderly disposal of surplus material; or
(c)	to facilitate the readjustment of industry and commerce to the requirements of the community in time of peace; or

Defence Production Act
(d)	to assist the relief of suffering and the restoration and distribution of essential supplies and services in any part of His Majesty's dominions or in foreign countries that are in grave distress as the result of war;
he may by order in council direct that the regulation shall have effect by virtue of this act . . .
And so forth. Now, those are the provisions in the legislation of the United Kingdom. I say to hon. members that they will search in vain for legislation comparable to the Defence Production Act, at the time of its passing, as to the powers it confers on the cabinet, or powers conferred upon a minister.
I urge that hon. members, before they vote these renewed and extended powers-because they will be extended in the sense that now they will be without limit in point of time-should ask themselves this question and apply this test. Are these powers necessary? Well, surely in the light of the fact that we are negotiating from strength today it is not going to be said, particularly in view of the statements made by the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs, that conditions are not improved over what they were in 1951. Therefore it is surely fair, in asking ourselves "Are these powers necessary today?" to ask what use was made of them, to ask what use the government and the minister found it necessary to make of them in the days of crisis, beginning in 1951.
What is the record? Well, the minister was asked some questions by myself in the house on March 11, at the resolution stage, as to the use which the government had found it necessary to make since 1951 of these sweeping and untrammelled powers conferred upon the cabinet and the minister by the sections of the act I have just quoted. Here are the statements of the minister as to section 23. He says, "There has been no resort to that section." Then as to section 24, he refers to the fact that there were priorities orders some time in 1951, 1952 and 1953, but acknowledges that two years ago the priorities system came to an end, and that accordingly no use had been made of the powers under that section for the last two years.
Then we went to section 30, and I asked the minister:
What orders are in effect under section 30?
The minister answered that there were none. Then we went on to section 31, and I asked if there were any orders outstanding under section 31 today, to which the minister replied that there were no orders outstanding at that time under section 31. Then I asked about prosecutions under section 32, and the minister said tonight that there were, altogether, nine prosecutions, and that the last conviction was entered on May 30, 1953.

So it is evident that there has been no occasion to use the powers under that section for the past two years.
Then the minister was also asked about section 27, which gives him the power to appoint a controller, and he admitted that the government did not find it necessary to use the power to appoint any controller. Then as to section 28, the minister has said tonight that the government has not invoked that section. It is evident again that the government did not find it necessary to use or invoke the extraordinary powers conveyed by that section. Similarly in regard to section 29, no use has been made of the powers to appoint a special investigator.
It is evident from this review that since those very trying days beginning in 1951 the government has not found it necessary to use more than a fragment of the powers the government now asks to be continued, and continued without any limitation whatsoever in point of time. The whole aggregate use made by the government and the minister of the powers under this act, the extent to which they found it necessary to resort to or invoke those powers, just falls infinitely short of justifying the sweeping powers under this act.
Sir, the minister himself gave away the whole case he was trying to make for an increase in those powers when he admitted this, as reported at page 1967 of Hansard:
X know of no one who does not take defence contracts, all the defence contracts they can get under this act; they are very glad to do so.
Sir, in the face of that statement how can the minister seriously ask this House of Commons to go on vesting in him sweeping powers which the government has not found any occasion to resort to or invoke in the very trying days behind us? The fact is that we are in a buyers' market today, and the minister well knows that. Industry well knows it. The minister has plainly admitted that he gets all the co-operation from industry that is required.
Now let us deal with one or two, indeed with all the arguments the minister has put forward in asking for this grant of powers. First of all, he has not told us explicitly but we know from past experience that the government always seeks to justify the granting of excessive powers to it, at the expense of parliament, by saying, "Oh, but we need stand-by powers." Sir, this government does not need stand-by powers.

speechtext: We did not say that, either.

speechtext:
The fact of the matter is that parliament is an existing institution. Parliament can be called together very swiftly. We remember very well August, 1950, when parliament, even in the face of a crippling national railway strike, was called together in a matter of several days. Members got here somehow or other in a matter of several days after being called; in much less time, indeed, than a week.
Is it to be said that such a calamity is going to befall this country under present conditions that, with reasonable powers under a proper measure of this kind, the interests of the country would suffer while parliament was being summoned? Sir, I say to you that, in face of the facts, that argument just does not hold water any more. But if a supreme calamity should befall this country, then I say the only supreme calamity which could justify these sweeping and untrammelled powers being conferred by parliament upon the cabinet would be a third world war, and we might as well be frank enough to acknowledge that fact. Canada has all the stand-by legislation it needs for that purpose under the provisions of the War Measures Act, chapter 288 of the revised statutes, which stands on the statute books of Canada. There are continuing powers. If that supreme calamity which, pray God, may never befall us, should come about, every power that Canada needs, the supreme power, is there at the government's hand, if it chooses to invoke that act under those extreme circumstances.
Therefore I say, sir, that the argument the government has used in times past about the need for stand-by legislation just does not hold water. On the contrary, the existence of legislation of this kind places in the hands of the minister-a minister who has never been unwilling to accept grants of power at the hands of parliament-powers that could be used to create compulsion, a compulsion of fear on the part of Canadian citizens.
Will hon. members recall the words used in the house by this same minister on September 8, 1950, when, in reference to the Essential Materials (Defence) Act, he said this:
I suggest to the committee that a word from the government is more effective if there is a law in the background that can be applied in case the response is not all that may be desired.
I suggest to you, sir, that there is a sinister meaning lurking in those words. And I say to you, sir, it is such a sinister possibility that the House of Commons ought to be supremely vigilant in not placing such powers in the hands of a minister as will permit him to hold a club over the head of any Canadian or a threat over the head of 50433-2851

Then there is the argument sometimes used in connection with this legislation, one we have heard in years past, that this legislation could be used by a beneficent government for the purpose of distributing the benefits of defence production. This was the measure that some members thought was going to be used to bring the benefits of secondary industry to the maritime provinces, for instance, or to take some defence construction to the prairie provinces. Well, sir, that was a very hollow and empty promise, as hon. members well know. I do not think any hon. member is likely to be deluded by that argument again.
Then in fairness I wish to recall that the minister did tell us when this measure was under discussion at the resolution stage-you will find it on page 1995 of Hansard-that we were faced in Canada today with shortages. He was apparently trying to chill the blood in the veins of hon. members as they recalled the scramble for the strategic materials that were in such short supply when this measure was first passed in March of 1951. The minister used these words:
As I have said, we have a shortage today of nickel. We have a shortage of copper. We have a shortage of aluminum, and we are threatened in Canada with a shortage of scrap iron.
Sir, what are the facts? The fact is that production of copper is running at record rates in Canada. The fact is, sir, that the same can be said of the production of nickel and of aluminum. Our exports of these metals are at record highs today. I do not suppose we have ever known anything like these figures in peacetime, and therefore in the face of the fact that Canada is exporting those metals at such a prodigious rate today, I do not think anybody is going to take very seriously the suggestion of the minister that we have a shortage of those commodities or metals in Canada today.
I appeal to hon. members, sir, and I do this respectfully and earnestly. Here I am not appealing to a minister whose mind is inflexible; I am appealing to hon. members who normally support the government, in the hope that they will individually take a serious and responsible look at what they are being invited to do. Here I am not dealing with something that is abstract or theoretical; it seems to me that in talking about the rights of parliament and the position of parliament as the champion of the rights and freedom of the people, we are talking about something that is more practical than anything else I know of.

Defence Production Act
The supreme duty of parliament, in discharging its responsibility to the people, is to be true and faithful to its traditional role of the champion of the rights and freedom of the people. I quote, sir:
The privileges of parliament are the privileges ox the people, and the rights of parliament are the rights of the people.
Sir, those are not my words. Those were the words of a greater Liberal than is to be found in the House of Commons today. These were the words of Edward Blake in his speech in London on August 28, 1873.
How this government loves to dress up what is in fact a denial of the rule of law, the subjugation of parliament to the executive branch of government, by having parliament go through the process of conferring upon them the power to legislate. And that vicious practice is dressed up. An attempt is made to clothe it with an air of respectability by calling it "delegated legislation". Sir, no euphonious title will succeed in applying a sufficient disguise to this vicious and threatening practice.
Hon. members can well see, in the light of the description of the Prime Minister of the powers under this act, that these are such powers as make it possible for the government to make itself dictator of the Canadian economy tomorrow. Under this legislation the government, and particularly the Minister of Defence Production, hold the Canadian economy in the palms of their hands. The government can override any other legal obligation howsoever created.
Sir, these powers are so sweeping that I am quite sure most Canadians just could not believe this is the way in which parliament is called upon by this government to legislate. But there are recent words by a very eminent Canadian Liberal whose political as well as professional views have been sought by this government, or have been made known to this government in more ways than one. I refer, sir, to a speech made in Toronto last Friday by Professor J. A. Corry of Queen's University, which was reported in the Toronto Globe and Mail, of June 3, 1955, and from which I draw a couple of paragraphs:
The events of the last 30 years have reinforced the attachment of the thoughtful to the rule of law. But the substance of the rule of law will not be preserved unless very substantial numbers of the electorate put a high value on individual freedom, feel a sense of personal responsibility for its maintenance, and are habituated by constant practice to steering their own course. This opinion was expressed last night by Professor J. A. Corry of Queen's University, president of the Canadian political science association, speaking on the prospects for the rule of law . . .
Dr. Corry outlined how the rule of law was threatened by the delegating by parliament to its

executive government of wide-reaching discretionary power. Special study was made of the situation in Britain, with detailed consideration of the Crichel Down case in which a bureaucratic decision was finally reversed after a long fight.
"No one knows how many Crichel Downs there really are over which village Hampdens failed to make any dent in the departmental armor," the speaker commented.
If discretionary powers of executive government are concerned with the margins of activity in which individuals and groups engage together, and not with the core and centre of the relationships, the community can hope to benefit by discretionary regulation. Dr. Corry believed. If, on the other hand, government has pulled down too many of the guiding signs that law provides, and replaced them with a promise of policy directives which cannot be predicted as to timing and which can be changed at will, the essential self-generating initiative which is the mark of the free community will be paralyzed.
"Where comprehensive planning and directing of economic and social life has been conceded to the government, the rule of law and its consequent individual freedoms cannot survive," the speaker stated.
Sir, these are not my words; these are not the words of any member of Her Majesty's loyal opposition. These are the words of a very eminent Canadian political thinker, and a Liberal, if you please. This is what he has to say about the practice of delegated legislation, this vicious and unwholesome practice in which we are being invited by the government to indulge again.
Sir, hon. members, as I conceive it, were elected to this house to legislate, not to abdicate the legislative function to the government. They are elected to preserve freedom, not to open the doors or admit the Trojan horse of executive power into the citadel of Canadian freedom.
We of Her Majesty's loyal opposition have fought this kind of legislation, and I think we can point to some success. And, sir, we mean to go on fighting against this vicious practice. Let there be no doubt in the mind of anyone on that score.
Sir, I address myself, I will not say hopefully but at least earnestly, to hon. members opposite who normally support the government and call themselves members of the Liberal majority in this house. I quote to them words which are not mine:
You are representatives of the people, and I put it to you, as you are greatly honoured, should you not greatly dare? You are sent to do your duty to your constituents, whether your acts always give satisfaction or not.
Sir, these are the words of Mr. Howe; not the Minister of Defence Production but the great Joseph Howe, than whom no Canadian had a greater understanding or perception of democracy, according to the British parliamentary tradition. Those were words addressed to the majority, that they should

do their duty whether they give satisfaction or not; in this case whether or not they give satisfaction to the government opposite.
And again:
Free and independent men in the legislature, as in the country, are the best counterpoise to faction and the mainspring of a nation's progress and greatness.
Those are the words of Egerton Ryerson, one of the greatest of all Canadians, uttered in 1867.
I give one more quotation. These are not the words of a Canadian, but they are worthy to be the words of any Canadian believer in democracy:
The most dangerous enemy to truth and freedom amongst us is the compact majority.
Those are the words of Henrik Ibsen, to be found in his "An Enemy of the People". I do not wish to take anything away from the position of the majority in this house, but I do ask hon. members who constitute the majority to ask themselves as individuals, after they have read, marked and inwardly digested the provisions of this bill, whether they are justified in removing the time limitation which parliament found it necessary to write into this legislation in a day of crisis in 1951, and continuing to grant all these powers without curb and without time limit.
Freedom is not something abstract and theoretical; it is something intensely practical. Not so many years ago there was a man who said:
It is true that liberty is precious-so precious that it must be rationed.
Some hon. members will recognize those as the words of Nikolai Lenin. In 1955 let the Canadian parliament not be a party to the rationing of that freedom which is embodied in the authority of parliament.
Hon. members have been asked to believe that it is necessary to do this, even in face of the fact that the government did not find it necessary to invoke more than a fragment of these powers in days more difficult than those we are living in now. I think of the words of William Pitt, who said:
Necessity is the plea for every infringement of human freedom; it is the argument of tyrants; it is the creed of slaves.
If things were different the government's case might be stronger, but we as members of this house cannot close our eyes to the fact that whether it is exercising extraordinary powers or even ordinary powers this government has set its face against communicating information to parliament which the elected representatives of the people ought to have. Indeed it has reached the
Defence Production Act point now where there is a veritable complex on this subject in the mind of the cabinet and of those who have supported it through thick and thin. Under those circumstances parliament is curbed; under those circumstances the great days of parliament are gone. It rests with us to decide whether we shall reverse this trend and restore something of the greatness of parliament. I quote again:
Parliament is the grand inquest which has the right to inquire into anything and everything.
Those were the words of a man who spent a great deal of his life holding ministerial power in Canada; those were words uttered in 1861 by Sir John A. Macdonald. In those days parliament was a grand inquest with the right to inquire into everything and anything, but it is not today, when we see secrecy imposed by the government, and hon. members of this house in the discharge of their solemn obligations to the constituents who elected them denied information they ought to have. Surely then hon. members are going to think seriously before they confer unlimited and untrammelled power upon this government without any limitation of time.
This is what I hope will be my final quotation:
Our objects are open and avowed. We seek no concealment, for we have nothing to conceal.
Those were the words of a great Liberal; those were words uttered by Robert Baldwin in 1844. That was the predominant and guiding principle in Liberal thought in those days, that Liberal governments having nothing to conceal should not make an effort to conceal. But this Liberal government in this year 1955 finds it necessary to conceal from the elected representatives of the people in parliament.
Our duty here is to restore the greatness of parliament. It is our duty to know what is required to be known by the people and their elected representatives, and above all to see that legislation that is to bind Canadians is passed in the open for all to see according to proper and established and traditional parliamentary processes.
The minister says, "Oh, it is enough that my estimates will be up every year." How can you repeal or amend legislation on the minister's estimates? The suggestion has nothing but nonsense in it. All you can do then is just discuss things in an amiable sort of way. Yet we are asked to say that that is an effective substitute for a statutory limitation of time on these powers.
The minister talks about the rule of law, and then admits that he does not understand very much about it. It was not necessary for him to make that open admission. If

Defence Production Act parliament is to go on conferring the right of delegated legislation, then we have in fact torn the rule of law to shreds and tatters. Make no mistake about that. Some hon. members may not realize that tonight, but the day well may come when they will realize it.
We are told by the minister that the Department of Justice having reviewed the bill says that it does not find it practical to introduce a limitation on the powers, or to limit the life of the powers. Is anybody going to take that kind of statement from the minister seriously? It will be taken no more seriously than were some of the other statements by which he sought tonight to lead us along this path toward the destruction of the rule of law. Presumably this is the same Department of Justice which in 1951 approved a measure that contained a very effective time limit which is to be done away with by this bill.
Then the minister says, "We must have all the powers or no Defence Production Act at all." What a typical statement; all or none! As far as the minister is concerned, it is all or none. There is no place here for even a limitation such as parliament thought it necessary to introduce in the days of crisis in 1951. No, it is all or none; all the power or none! We know what the choice of the minister will be as between all the power or none; it will be all the power.
We have had opportunities in this house during the past decade to see what power does for people. How often I have thought of those words with which Shakespeare described Cleopatra:
-other women cloy
The appetites they feed, but she makes hungry
Where most she satisfies;
The possession of power does not satisfy the appetite for power; it whets the appetite for more power. We have seen that in this government. We have seen that in this minister. The appetite has proved insatiable. Now when some powers the government has had are about to come to an end by the lapse of time the government's slogan is: what we have, we hold.
Mr. Speaker, the position of Her Majesty's loyal opposition is this, and I emphasize it again. We support the continuation on a permanent basis of the Department of Defence Production. We are prepared to give the government what powers are adequate to meet any proven existing need, or any that can be measured within the foreseeable future under present conditions, bearing in mind that parliament is never far away and can be called at any time if the government needs it. According to our view, these powers

must be clearly defined and must be commensurate with a proven need. So far as we are concerned there will be no wholesale abdication on the part of parliament to satisfy a ministerial appetite for power.
May I remind the house that this legislation dates from the very time parliament passed the Emergency Powers Act. Indeed that act was passed in the same month-March, 1951. That legislation conferred upon the cabinet the most extraordinary powers, indeed everything the cabinet would derive from a proclamation under the War Measures Act except power to arrest, detain and deport the person. That legislation, however, had in it a safeguard which was thought to be wise and necessary. It was the safeguard of a short time limit, which compelled the government to come back to the house two years later and again, year after year, before it received an extension of these powers. That was a sound precedent in any case where any powers that have any reason to be described as extraordinary are voted to the cabinet by parliament.
Why should not that precedent be observed here, Mr. Speaker? You will recall that the Prime Minister on April 29, 1954, when he was asked if the government was going to ask parliament to renew those powers for another year, said this, as reported at page 4229 of Hansard:
. .	. we have come to the conclusion we will
not at this session ask parliament to extend the Emergency Powers Act. We felt it was a grave decision to make because there is still a pretty explosive situation existing in the world. I hope the situation will not require the exercise of any but normal powers by the governor in council. But should it develop that there would have to be, in the interests of the safety of the nation, powers exercised that are not normally conferred upon the governor in council by existing legislation, we would have to resort to the War Measures Act. I sincerely hope that will never be necessary while X am a member of the government.
Every hon. member in this house will hope that it will never be necessary to invoke those powers. But note, Mr. Speaker, that a year ago, before the world situation had undergone the improvement that happily it has undergone in the intervening year, the Prime Minister then was saying that conditions had improved so far in 1954 over those in 1951 that that extraordinary legislation conferring these wide, sweeping powers could be allowed to lapse; and second, he recognized that stand-by legislation was available to meet any supreme need that might arise. How can hon. members then treat seriously any suggestion that it is now necessary to do away with the time limitation on the powers conferred by this measure? Words of this kind have a hollow ring today.

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I say that the issue here is deep-seated, clear-cut and fundamental. It is the issue of the rule of law and the preservation of the authority of parliament. It is not simply a matter of the preservation of the form of parliament but the preservation of the substance of parliamentary authority and rule. We will have nothing to do with the grant of powers vastly in excess of need. We will not be parties to embedding permanently in the statute law of Canada sweeping and extraordinary powers so wide that they would not need to be widened for the purpose of defence production even in the event of a third world war, according to the Prime Minister's own definition. We will not do this to indulge the government's appetite for power.
This theory of the strong executive, so far as we are concerned, must be regarded with certain limitations. The very learned author of the book entitled "The Passing of Parliament", namely Professor G. W. Keeton, dean of the faculty of law at University College, London, England, in his chapter entitled "The Road to Moscow" points out that there are three principal attributes of the Soviet system. They are as follows:
(1) a one-party organization in which, although there is a wide power of criticism within the party, no external opposition is tolerated: (2) an all-powerful executive, which can put into effect the program decided upon by the party, without substantial impediment or modification, especially that which might emanate from an independent parliament, and (3) an economy which is moulded within the framework of a comprehensive plan, and in which all the more significant activities are government monopolies, subservient only to executive control.
Defence Production Act
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that while the government cannot be said to subscribe to the first of those attributes except in so far as it is permitting the other place to die by neglect, nevertheless the government is going overboard in the direction of the all-powerful executive and carrying with it the danger of the third attribute, namely the organization of the economy within the framework of a comprehensive plan. That may suit the philosophy of some parties in this country such as those with a socialist view; but, Mr. Speaker, it does not suit the philosophy of the Conservative party. So far as we are concerned there are higher authorities than these; there are higher principles and higher standards to guide the legislators in the Canadian democracy. Supreme over any all-powerful executive, in our view, must stand the authority of a free, sovereign and independent parliament.
